hazards.name: Large asteroid impact (≥1 km near-Earth asteroid)
hazards.oneLine: A kilometre-class stony or iron near-Earth asteroid strikes Earth, lofting enough fine dust and soot into the stratosphere to suppress photosynthesis and destroy one or more global growing seasons.
hazards.mechanism: A ≥1 km asteroid arriving at ~20 km/s deposits 10^4–10^6 Mt of kinetic energy in seconds; the crater excavates and vaporises target rock, and the rising plume injects micrometre-scale silicate dust into the stratosphere, while thermal radiation from re-entering ejecta ignites wildfires that add soot. The blast, tsunami and thermal pulse kill regionally — hundreds of kilometres — and are not the global mechanism. The global mechanism is optical: Senel et al. (2023) show that fine silicate dust in the ~0.8–8.0 μm range has an atmospheric lifetime of order 15 years and, for the Chicxulub loading, drove global-average surface temperature down by as much as 15 °C and shut photosynthesis down for almost two years. Sub-Chicxulub impacts scale this down but the qualitative chain is the same: reduced photosynthetically active radiation plus surface cooling plus shortened frost-free season equals simultaneous harvest failure across the northern-hemisphere breadbaskets. Xia et al. (2022) calibrate the human end of that chain for stratospheric soot: injections above 5 Tg already cause mass food shortages that livestock and fisheries cannot offset, and a 150 Tg injection leaves more than 5 billion people without enough calories. People die of famine, in the second and third years, in countries that were never near the crater.

rate.eventDefinition: impact on Earth by a near-Earth asteroid of diameter ≥1 km — the long-run background rate from the telescopic size-frequency distribution and collision probability, NOT adjusted for the fact that ~95% of this population is already catalogued and known to be clear for the next century
rate.trend: The background arrival rate is flat on any human timescale. The rate of an UNWARNED ≥1 km impact is falling steeply and is now roughly 20x below the background rate: ~95% of ≥1 km NEOs are catalogued (NASEM 2023 decadal, Ch.18) and JPL Sentry currently lists only two objects at Palermo scale ≥ −2 — Bennu (0.49 km, cumulative impact probability 5.7e-4) and 29075 (1950 DA, 1.3 km, 3.77e-4) — neither of which threatens Earth this century. For the 140 m class the trend is also downward but far less advanced: 11,584 NEAs with H<22.0 are catalogued out of an estimated ~25,000, and NEO Surveyor (launch no earlier than 2027) is intended to close that gap.

tiers.label: Regional catastrophe, no sustained impact winter
tiers.desc: A 1–1.5 km body, or an ocean strike, or a strike on sparsely populated land. Crater, tsunami and thermal pulse devastate a region; stratospheric dust loading stays below the threshold for multi-season global crop failure. NRC (2010) conservatively places the global-catastrophe threshold at 1.5 km diameter, so most of the ≥1 km distribution sits below it.
tiers.split: regional: blast, tsunami and thermal pulse, all of it prompt and none of it buffered by a grain reserve

tiers.label: Impact winter with global harvest failure
tiers.desc: A 1.5–5 km body. Dust plus wildfire soot in the stratosphere for years; photosynthetically active radiation and growing-season length both cut across the whole northern hemisphere. Deaths are overwhelmingly from famine in years 2–4, not from the impact. Death fraction anchored on Xia et al. (2022), where a 150 Tg stratospheric soot injection leaves >5 billion of ~8 billion people short of calories; a few-kilometre impact plausibly sits an order of magnitude below that loading.
tiers.split: the prompt toll is unchanged — the extra 29% is famine, from stratospheric dust suppressing photosynthesis

tiers.label: Chicxulub-class
tiers.desc: A ≥5 km body. Senel et al. (2023) parameters apply directly: ~15 year dust lifetime, up to 15 °C global cooling, ~2 years of effectively no photosynthesis. Agriculture is impossible for several consecutive years anywhere on Earth. Survival depends on stored food, fisheries, and non-photosynthetic (resilient) food production, none of which currently exists at scale.
tiers.split: Senel et al. 2023 put fine silicate dust lifetime at ~15 years and photosynthesis shutdown at ~2 years for Chicxulub loading

tiers.label: Terminal
tiers.desc: The residual case in which no self-sustaining human population persists through the winter and the subsequent centuries. Note that mammals, birds and crocodilians survived Chicxulub; humanity is far more capable than a Cretaceous mammal but also far more dependent on a functioning grain system. This tier is an author-estimate residual, not a measured quantity.

hazards.uncertainty: WEAKEST POINTS, in order. (1) The severity tiers are the soft part of this entry. The three probabilities I report are of different kinds and must not be conflated: the EVENT rate (~1.7e-6/yr for ≥1 km) is well constrained by the telescopic size-frequency distribution and the cratering record and is probably good to a factor of ~1.5; the CONDITIONAL death fractions are author-estimates anchored on a soot-to-famine curve (Xia et al. 2022) that was built for nuclear war, not for impacts, and the mapping from impactor diameter to stratospheric dust and soot loading in Tg is exactly the step I could not find a published, quantitative, sub-Chicxulub curve for. A serious critic should attack the 0.30 deaths_fraction in the impact-winter tier first; it is a judgement, not a measurement. (2) The p_given_event split between tiers is derived by interpolating the size-frequency distribution between two retrieved anchors (1 km every ~520,000 yr, 10 km every ~100 Myr, implying P(≥10 km | ≥1 km) ≈ 0.005) with an assumed D^-2.5 slope; the slope is not itself cited here. (3) The terminal tier (p = 0.002 given a ≥1 km event, i.e. ~3.4e-9/yr) is a pure author-estimate. Ord's The Precipice (2020, Table 6.1) is widely reported as giving ~1 in 1,000,000 per century for asteroid/comet existential catastrophe — I could NOT retrieve the table itself this session, only secondary summaries, so I have deliberately excluded it from the citation list. My figure implies ~3.4e-7 per century for terminal outcomes from ≥1 km asteroids, i.e. about 3x below the reported Ord number; that is agreement within the noise of this kind of estimate, but I am not treating it as corroboration. (4) The two completeness figures for ≥1 km disagree slightly: dividing the live catalogue (867 with H<17.75) by Harris & D'Abramo's population estimate of 920 gives 94%, matching the decadal survey's '~95 percent', but the H<17.75 to 1 km conversion assumes an albedo of 0.14 and dark objects are systematically under-counted. Real completeness for ≥1 km is probably a few percent lower than the headline. (5) The 46% completeness I compute for ≥140 m divides a live H<22.0 count by a population estimate from a different source and a different epoch; the sources I retrieved that state completeness directly say 'about one third' (2019 and 2021 vintage) and one modelling paper says ~38%. 46% is the most current number but is the least cleanly sourced of the completeness figures. (6) NEO Surveyor is currently no earlier than September 2027 per NASA reporting; I did not fetch a NASA mission page confirming this and have not used it as a cited figure.

hazards.name: Long-period comet impact
hazards.oneLine: A comet nucleus from the Oort cloud, discovered only months to a couple of years before arrival, strikes Earth at roughly twice the speed of an asteroid — the residual impact risk that no survey can retire in advance.
hazards.mechanism: A long-period comet spends essentially all of its orbit beyond detection range and becomes visible only on the inbound leg, typically inside a few AU. Comet Siding Spring, the standard case study, was discovered on 3 January 2013 and reached Mars on 22 October 2014 — 22 months of warning, and that was for a close approach, not a collision with a body being tracked toward Earth. If such an object is on an Earth-impacting trajectory the physical outcome is the asteroid impact-winter chain but harder: meteor-stream proxies give a median comet encounter velocity of 39.5 km/s against ~20 km/s for asteroids, so an equal-mass comet delivers ~3.9x the kinetic energy, and Nuth et al. put a typical comet impact at 50–100x the energy of a typical asteroid impact. More energy at higher altitude means more fine silicate dust and vaporised material injected higher into the stratosphere, where the ~15-year dust lifetime measured for Chicxulub applies. The kill mechanism is identical to the asteroid case — years of suppressed photosynthetically active radiation, cooling, growing-season loss and famine — but the response window is measured in months, and the NRC found that long-period-comet intercept trajectories typically permit only a ~0.5 tonne payload, which is 'sufficient for a nuclear package but rather small for a kinetic impactor'. DART-style deflection is therefore essentially inapplicable to this hazard.

rate.eventDefinition: impact on Earth by a long-period comet nucleus of diameter ≥1 km (orbital period >200 years, i.e. dynamically new or near-new Oort-cloud objects)
rate.trend: Flat to very slightly falling. Unlike asteroids, this rate cannot be retired by surveying: the population is not resident in the inner solar system and cannot be catalogued in advance. Wide-field surveys (Rubin/LSST, NEO Surveyor's comet sensitivity) will push the typical detection distance outward and so lengthen warning time from months toward a few years, which reduces the CONSEQUENCE-weighted risk without changing the arrival rate at all. This is the irreducible residual: as asteroid completeness rises toward 90–95%+, long-period comets become a progressively larger share of the remaining unwarned impact risk.

rateMods.why: a dynamically new comet arrives with months of warning, not decades: the NRC found intercepts permit only ~0.5-tonne payloads, so only a standing pre-built interceptor helps at all, and the survey knob does nothing whatsoever — these objects are not in any catalogue by construction

hazards.uncertainty: WEAKEST POINTS, in order. (1) The annual probability is the weakest number in this entire packet. It is not measured; it is constructed by taking the ≥1 km asteroid rate (~1.7e-6/yr, well sourced) and multiplying by a rate ratio of ~1/100 that comes from two independent statements — the NRC/decadal '<1 percent of total risk' and Nuth et al.'s '100 times less likely' — which happen to agree numerically but are not the same quantity: one is a RISK share, the other a RATE ratio. If the NRC's <1% is risk-weighted (i.e. already includes the energy multiplier), then the true rate ratio is nearer 1/300 to 1/1000 and my best estimate is high by up to an order of magnitude. I have widened low/high to 5e-9–1e-7 to cover this, but a critic should attack this construction first. There is no direct observational determination of the long-period-comet Earth-impact rate in anything I retrieved — the observed sample of LPC Earth impacts is zero. (2) The NRC/decadal figure (~1%) and Nuth et al. (~50% of destructive threat) genuinely disagree about how large this hazard is, by a factor of ~50. I have exposed that as a tunable knob rather than silently picking one. A model that adopts Nuth's convention should expect this hazard's expected-mortality contribution to approach that of asteroids despite the far lower rate. (3) The severity tier probabilities are author-estimates. There is no published comet-specific size-frequency distribution in what I retrieved, so the split across tiers is inferred from the asteroid distribution shifted upward by the velocity-energy factor (39.5 vs 20 km/s → 3.9x energy → roughly one size-class shift). That inference is mine, not a citation. (4) The '22 months' warning figure is a single case study (Siding Spring, a Mars close approach, not an Earth impactor), used by Nuth et al. as their exemplar. It is not a distribution. Real warning times for an impacting LPC could plausibly range from a few weeks to several years depending on nucleus size, activity onset distance, and survey cadence; treating 22 months as a median is an assumption. (5) The 0.3–0.6 'deflectable fraction with a standing interceptor' quoted in the interceptor knob is an author-estimate with no source; it should be treated as a placeholder for a proper mission-design study. (6) I could not retrieve Ord's The Precipice Table 6.1 or the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament report at source this session (the XPT working paper exceeded the fetch size limit and the Precipice table exists only as an image in the sources I could reach), so no expert-elicitation figure is cited in this packet. Secondary reporting puts Ord's asteroid/comet existential estimate at ~1 in 1,000,000 per century and the XPT's non-anthropogenic extinction estimate at ~0.004% by 2100 with experts and superforecasters in near-agreement; I have deliberately NOT dressed either as a citation, and a follow-up pass should retrieve both at source.

hazards.name: Mainline anthropogenic warming (chronic damage)
hazards.oneLine: Continued greenhouse-gas forcing warms the planet by roughly 1.4–4.4 °C by 2100 depending on emissions pathway, killing people chronically through heat, food-system stress and conflict rather than in a single event.
hazards.mechanism: Radiative forcing from accumulated CO2 and other greenhouse gases raises global mean surface temperature; AR6 assesses 1.09 °C of warming already realised over 2011–2020 relative to 1850–1900. The warming does not kill directly at the global scale — it shifts the distribution of heat, drought, flood and growing-season conditions. The dominant proximate killers are (a) direct heat mortality in hot, poor, low-adaptive-capacity regions, which Carleton et al. quantify at an additional 85 deaths per 100,000 per year by 2100 under RCP8.5 after netting adaptation benefits against adaptation costs, and (b) food-price and food-availability shocks when major breadbaskets fail in the same year. Gaupp et al. show the annual probability of simultaneous climate risk across all major breadbaskets already rose between 1967–1990 and 1991–2012 (wheat 0.3% to 1.2%). Kornhuber et al. show that the jet-stream meander states that drive synchronous Northern-Hemisphere harvest failures are systematically under-reproduced by bias-adjusted crop and climate models, so the modelled tail of simultaneous failure is too thin. Mass death in this hazard is famine and heat, mediated by markets and governments, not drowning or storms.

rate.eventDefinition: The chronic hazard is ACTIVE in any given year — i.e. anthropogenic warming continues to accumulate and impose damage. This is not a stochastic event: AR6 assesses human influence on warming as unequivocal and 2011–2020 as 1.09 °C above 1850–1900. In a simulator the SSP knob must set the MAGNITUDE of damage, not the probability of occurrence.
rate.trend: Severity rising, probability flat at ~1. Under SSP2-4.5 (best estimate 2.7 °C by 2081–2100) damage roughly doubles per ~0.6 °C of additional warming in the 2.7–4.4 °C band, inferred from the two Carleton mortality points. Probability of the hazard being active cannot rise above 1.

sevMods.why: damage tracks REALISED warming rather than a scenario label, so the emissions and sensitivity knobs reach it. Reference is 2.7 °C — the AR6 SSP2-4.5 figure the tier table is written against — so at that warming the model reproduces the cited numbers exactly. Exponent 1.6 because heat mortality and yield loss both rise faster than linearly

tiers.label: Paris-consistent (~1.8 °C)
tiers.desc: SSP1-2.6 pathway; 1.8 °C best estimate (very likely 1.3–2.4 °C) by 2081–2100. Coral reefs are lost and regional impacts are severe, but global excess mortality stays an order of magnitude below the high-emissions case. Deaths fraction is a 10-year cumulative excess-mortality figure near 2100, extrapolated below Carleton's RCP4.5 point.
tiers.split: 40% prompt (heat, flood, vector-borne), 60% via food. Tabulated over ten years and spread accordingly

tiers.label: Current-policy (~2.7 °C)
tiers.desc: SSP2-4.5 pathway; 2.7 °C best estimate (very likely 2.1–3.5 °C) by 2081–2100. Carleton et al. put RCP4.5 full mortality risk about 84% below the RCP8.5 figure, i.e. roughly 14 additional deaths per 100,000 per year by 2100; over ten years that is ~0.14% of population. Several Armstrong McKay tipping thresholds are exceeded on the way, which is why this hazard cascades into the tail entry.
tiers.split: same split

tiers.label: High emissions (~3.6–4.4 °C)
tiers.desc: SSP3-7.0 to SSP5-8.5; 3.6 °C (2.8–4.6) to 4.4 °C (3.3–5.7) by 2081–2100. Carleton et al.: an additional 85 deaths per 100,000 annually by 2100 under RCP8.5 including adaptation costs, i.e. ~0.85% of population over a decade. This is a mortality-only figure; it excludes famine, conflict and displacement deaths.
tiers.split: same split

tiers.label: High emissions with food-system failure
tiers.desc: High-end warming coinciding with repeated multi-breadbasket failure and the conflict/displacement channel that Carleton's mortality-only estimate excludes. Author-estimate: the excess over the pure-heat figure is not published as a single number. Severe regional state failure, no global industrial collapse.
tiers.split: the food-system-failure tier tips toward famine: 20% prompt

cascades.why: every tenth of a degree raises the probability of crossing a threshold; Armstrong McKay et al. place several central thresholds inside the mainline range
Gaupp et al. measure synchronous multi-breadbasket failure probability rising from 0.3% to 1.2% per year as warming proceeded
Kemp et al. name conflict as one of four proximate mass-mortality pathways; the coupling is real and the magnitude is contested, so it is kept small

hazards.uncertainty: Three weaknesses a serious critic would attack. (1) The IPCC figures were NOT retrieved from ipcc.ch — every direct fetch of the AR6 SPM PDF and HTML returned HTTP 403 this session — so Table SPM.1, the ECS ranges and the 1.09 °C observed-warming figure come from Carbon Brief's reproduction of them. They match my prior knowledge of AR6 exactly, but the chain of custody is one hop longer than ideal and a reviewer should re-verify against IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf. I could not retrieve the very likely range on the 1.09 °C figure at all. (2) The mortality figures are heat-mortality only. Carleton et al. explicitly value temperature-driven mortality net of adaptation; they do NOT include famine, conflict, displacement, vector-borne disease, or sea-level-rise deaths. Using their 85/100,000/yr as the total death rate at 4.4 °C is therefore a LOWER bound, and my fourth severity tier's 0.04 deaths fraction is an author-estimate with no published anchor. (3) The exponential fit m(T) = 14 * 2^((T-2.7)/0.65) is my own two-point interpolation between Carleton's RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 results; the underlying paper does not publish that functional form, and it should not be extrapolated below 2 °C or above 4.5 °C. Also note the honest shape: this hazard has probability ~1 and severity that is large in absolute deaths but small as a fraction of world population within any decade. It is a near-certain major harm, not a plausible extinction cause; a simulator that treats it as a Poisson event with a small rate has the shape wrong.

hazards.name: Tipping cascade / high-sensitivity climate tail
hazards.oneLine: The badly-studied upper tail in which high climate sensitivity, a strong carbon-cycle feedback, or a cascade of crossed tipping elements pushes warming past 3 °C and breaks food systems and habitability over large regions.
hazards.mechanism: Armstrong McKay et al. identify sixteen tipping elements whose central thresholds cluster low: Greenland Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C, West Antarctic Ice Sheet ~1.5 °C, tropical coral reefs ~1.5 °C, widespread abrupt permafrost thaw ~1.5 °C, Labrador–Irminger Sea convection ~1.5–2 °C. Crossing them commits multi-metre sea-level rise over centuries and, in the permafrost case, amplifies permafrost carbon emissions by roughly 50%, which feeds back into warming. Higher up sit Amazon dieback (~3.5 °C) and AMOC shutdown (central ~4 °C, range 1–8 °C); an AMOC collapse would cool north-west Europe abruptly while disrupting monsoons that feed billions. The kill chain is not the ice or the current: it is agriculture. Kemp et al. name famine and undernutrition, extreme weather, conflict, and vector-borne disease as the Four Horsemen, and project that areas with annual mean temperature above 29 °C — home to about 30 million people today — will hold about 2 billion by 2070 under SSP3-7.0, overlapping two nuclear powers and seven maximum-containment laboratories. Wet-bulb limits set the outer bound on habitability: Vecellio et al.'s empirical critical limit of 30.55 ± 0.98 °C in humid conditions is well below Sherwood & Huber's theoretical 35 °C, so uninhabitable-by-heat conditions arrive at lower warming than the classic figure implies. Extinction, as opposed to catastrophe, is not a mechanism anyone has demonstrated; it would require the food system to fail globally and permanently, which no retrieved study models.

rate.eventDefinition: Onset, in a given year during the 21st century, of the 'extreme climate change' regime as Kemp et al. define it — mean global surface temperature rise of 3 °C or more above preindustrial by 2100 — TOGETHER with the crossing of three or more core tipping elements. Best estimate corresponds to about 14% over the century; the range spans about 3% to 40% per century.
rate.trend: Rising through mid-century then pathway-dependent. Under SSP2-4.5's 2.7 °C best estimate the low-threshold elements (~1.5 °C) are crossed regardless; the >3 °C condition is what the emissions and sensitivity knobs control. Under SSP1-2.6 (1.8 °C) the >3 °C condition is very unlikely and this hazard's rate falls by roughly an order of magnitude.

rateMods.why: steeply rising in realised warming — the whole content of Armstrong McKay et al. is that thresholds are crossed at particular temperatures, and most of the global core ones sit between 1.5 and 4 °C — reference point solved at build time (2.896) so that the mean multiplier over 100 years is exactly 1: the cited rate was annualised from a by-2100 figure, so its century total must be preserved while the shape is allowed to rise
a higher climate sensitivity reaches every threshold sooner; AR6 gives a very likely range of 2–5 °C around a best estimate of 3

tiers.label: Cascade without decimation
tiers.desc: Several core elements cross. Multi-metre sea-level rise is committed but plays out over centuries; coral fisheries collapse; permafrost feedback adds warming. Adaptation and trade absorb the food shocks. Large regional harm, large economic loss, no global mass-mortality event within a decade.
tiers.split: cascade without decimation — almost entirely food and displacement, so 15% prompt

tiers.label: Global decimation (Kemp et al. threshold)
tiers.desc: Kemp et al.'s 'Global Decimation Risk': loss of 10% or more of global population and severe disruption of global critical systems such as food, within a given timeframe. Mechanism is repeated multi-breadbasket failure plus conflict and displacement in the 29 °C-plus belt, not the tipping events themselves.
tiers.split: Kemp et al.'s decimation threshold; still famine-dominated

tiers.label: Global catastrophe (Kemp et al. GCR threshold)
tiers.desc: Kemp et al.'s 'Global Catastrophic Risk': loss of 25% of the global population and severe disruption of global critical systems. Requires the climate shock to compound with war, financial and state collapse — the 'catastrophe convergence' the Climate Endgame paper argues is under-studied. Industrial capacity survives but is set back for generations.
tiers.split: their global-catastrophe threshold

tiers.label: Terminal
tiers.desc: Humanity does not recover. No retrieved study demonstrates a mechanism by which climate change alone does this; Sherwood & Huber's 11–12 °C figure (majority of the currently-distributed human population in regions exceeding the 35 °C wet-bulb limit) is the nearest thing to a physical route, and it requires warming far above any SSP best estimate. The number here is anchored on Ord's elicited 1-in-1,000-per-century existential estimate divided by this hazard's per-century rate.
tiers.split: the tail. No sunLoss on any tier: climate catastrophe is a warming mechanism, not an aerosol one, and pretending otherwise would let a grain reserve buy more than it should

cascades.why: multi-breadbasket failure is the actual famine mechanism Kemp et al. identify
Kemp et al. note the projected 29 °C-plus belt in 2070 overlaps two nuclear-armed states
Kemp et al. note seven maximum-containment laboratories fall in areas of rising climate hazard; a weak coupling, kept weak

audit.claim: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022 Science 377:eabn7950 - tipping element central thresholds, ranges, timescales and classification
audit.note: This is the packet's serious citation failure - the paper is real, the authors and DOI are right, but roughly two thirds of the transcribed table is wrong, and the errors are not rounding. Worst: southern boreal forest dieback given as ~2 C (1-3) vs published 4.0 (1.4-5.0); northern boreal expansion ~2-3 C (1-4) vs 4.0 (1.5-7.2); Barents Sea ice ~2 C (1-3) vs 1.6 (1.5-1.7); Arctic winter sea ice ~5+ C (3-8) vs 6.3 (4.5-8.7); Yedoma/boreal permafrost collapse ~3-4 C (2-5) vs 4.0 (3.0-6.0). AMOC is given as a central BAND '~3-5 C' where the paper gives a point estimate 4.0 (1.4-8.0). Ranges are clipped throughout (Greenland low end 1 vs 0.8; Amazon high end 5 vs 6; Labrador-Irminger high end 3 vs 3.8; abrupt permafrost thaw high end 3 vs 2.3; mountain glaciers 1-4 vs 1.5-3.0; Sahel 1-4 vs 2.0-3.5). The global-core/regional classification is also scrambled: coral reefs, abrupt permafrost thaw and southern boreal dieback are listed as global core but are REGIONAL IMPACT elements in the paper, while Arctic winter sea ice and boreal permafrost collapse are listed as regional but are GLOBAL CORE - and the East Antarctic Ice Sheet, a global core element, is missing from the packet entirely. This matters directly to the hazard: the event is defined as 'three or more core tipping elements crossed', and the packet has miscounted which elements are core. Separately, the retrieval claim is not reproducible: I fetched https://climatetippingpoints.info/2022/09/09/climate-tipping-points-reassessment-explainer/ and Table 1 is present only as an IMAGE with no extractable numbers, so the stated provenance ('threshold table retrieved from the lead author's own paper explainer') cannot have produced these figures as text. Corrected values above cross-checked against the reproduction at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipping_points_in_the_climate_system, sourced to Armstrong McKay et al. 2022. Sea-level figures (Greenland 7+ m, WAIS 3-4 m, EASB 10+ m) I could not verify from any retrievable text; the 10+ m for the East Antarctic subglacial basins looks high and should be re-sourced before use.
audit.corrected: Greenland 1.5 (0.8-3.0); WAIS 1.5 (1.0-3.0); Labrador-Irminger/SPG 1.8 (1.1-3.8); East Antarctic subglacial basins 3.0 (2.0-6.0); Arctic winter sea ice 6.3 (4.5-8.7) [GLOBAL CORE]; East Antarctic Ice Sheet 7.5 (5.0-10.0) [GLOBAL CORE, omitted entirely]; Amazon 3.5 (2.0-6.0); boreal permafrost collapse 4.0 (3.0-6.0) [GLOBAL CORE]; AMOC 4.0 (1.4-8.0); coral reefs 1.5 (1.0-2.0) [REGIONAL]; permafrost abrupt thaw 1.5 (1.0-2.3) [REGIONAL]; Barents Sea ice 1.6 (1.5-1.7); mountain glaciers 2.0 (1.5-3.0); Sahel/W African monsoon 2.8 (2.0-3.5); boreal forest southern dieback 4.0 (1.4-5.0); boreal forest northern expansion 4.0 (1.5-7.2)

hazards.uncertainty: This is the weakest entry in the packet and should be labelled as such in any UI. (1) The annual probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE with no published anchor. No retrieved source gives a probability for a multi-element tipping cascade. I could not obtain climate-specific numbers from the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament: the report PDF exceeded the fetch size limit, the Forecasting Research Institute landing page and the EA Forum sequence contain no climate row, and my WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could reach the per-domain table. So the only elicitation anchor here is Ord's 1-in-1,000-per-century existential figure, from which I back out p(terminal | tail) = 0.005. A critic who thinks Ord's figure is too high or too low moves my terminal tier proportionally, and they would be right to. (2) The tipping thresholds are from the lead author's own explainer, not from the Science paper's Table 1 directly (paywalled). The explainer's AMOC figure reads '~3–5 °C central, 1–8 °C range'; I have seen the paper cited elsewhere as a 4.0 °C best estimate with a 1.4–8.0 °C range, and a reviewer should check Table 1 before compiling. (3) Armstrong McKay's thresholds carry LOW confidence in the paper itself for most elements — a critic would attack any simulator that treats them as sharp step functions, which is exactly why the tipping_threshold_offset knob exists. (4) The AMOC hazard rate of 0.3%/yr is mine, not anyone's: IPCC AR6 says a full 21st-century collapse is unlikely, Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen imply roughly 1.4%/yr, and their result is genuinely contested — the estimator is a highly idealised stochastic differential equation fitted to a sea-surface-temperature fingerprint proxy, the direct AMOC observational record only starts in 2004, and the authors themselves say 'we don't have an explanation for the outcome we observe'. A 2025 Author Correction moved the tipping-time estimate by 8 years, which is itself a signal of how sensitive the result is. (5) The wet_bulb_limit knob's mapping to global warming is UNMEASURED: Sherwood & Huber's 7 °C figure is for the 35 °C limit, and no retrieved source gives the equivalent warming for Vecellio's 30.6 °C limit. Do not fit a curve there. (6) Most important for honesty in both directions: the terminal tier is small on purpose. Kemp et al.'s whole argument is that this tail is UNDER-STUDIED, not that it is probable — they call it 'dangerously underexplored', which is a claim about our ignorance, not a probability. Nothing retrieved this session demonstrates a physical mechanism by which climate change alone permanently ends humanity below roughly 11–12 °C of warming, which is above every SSP best estimate including SSP5-8.5's 4.4 °C.

hazards.name: Deliberate release of an engineered pandemic pathogen
hazards.oneLine: A state programme or small group deliberately releases a pathogen modified to be more transmissible, more lethal, or harder to counter than anything circulating naturally.
hazards.mechanism: A deliberately released respiratory-transmissible pathogen spreads through travel networks faster than surveillance detects it; the defining feature versus a natural pandemic is that the attacker chooses the trait combination (transmissibility, incubation period, case fatality, countermeasure evasion) rather than accepting the trade-offs evolution imposes, and can seed many locations simultaneously rather than at one index point. Direct infection deaths are only the first term. The larger term is the collapse of the systems that keep eight billion people alive: healthcare workers are among the first infected and hospitals fail as staffing collapses; ports, freight, refineries and fertiliser plants stop when absenteeism passes a threshold, and food-exporting countries impose export bans. Historically famine, untreated ordinary illness, and loss of clean water kill more than the epidemic agent itself in a collapse. Extinction from any single agent is not the expected path even in the worst tiers — pockets of survivors are geographically isolated and infection eventually burns out — so a terminal outcome requires either multiple simultaneous agents (Esvelt's 'many pandemic viruses across travel hubs' scenario) or a permanent loss of the industrial base that prevents recovery. This is why Ord's ~3% existential figure is far below his implied probability that such an event occurs at all.

rate.eventDefinition: deliberate release of a genetically engineered pathogen that kills more than 1% of the world's human population within a five-year window
rate.trend: Rising. The number of actors able to attempt this is increasing as gene synthesis costs fall and AI biodesign tools diffuse; Esvelt (2022) argues that within roughly a decade tens of thousands of individuals will hold the necessary information, versus a handful of state programmes historically. Countervailing downward pressure comes from synthesis screening (IGSC ~80% coverage), the 2024 US OSTP screening framework, and the AI-screening patches deployed after Wittmann et al. (2025). Net direction is up on capability diffusion, ambiguous on defence — Ord's own 2023 revisit calls the pandemic story 'mixed'.

square-root rather than linear in the capability index. tiers.label: Severe global pandemic

tiers.label: Catastrophic pandemic

tiers.label: Civilisational collapse

hazards.uncertainty: Three distinct quantities must not be conflated and are separated above: (a) probability the release EVENT occurs at the >=1%-mortality threshold (my 5e-4 to 1.4e-3 per year, taken directly from the XPT medians spread over 2022-2100); (b) probability of a catastrophic outcome given the event (the tier distribution); (c) probability of permanent human extinction (annual rate = 8e-4 x 0.005 = 4e-6/yr, i.e. ~0.04% per century). THAT LAST NUMBER IS THE WEAKEST POINT AND IT DISAGREES WITH ORD BY ~80x. Ord's Table 6.1 gives 1 in 30 per century (~3.3%) for the existential outcome specifically; my parameterisation sits between the XPT superforecaster median (0.01%/century) and the XPT domain-expert median (1%/century), and below all of them. A serious critic will attack this from either direction: Ord's defenders will say my p(terminal | catastrophic event) of 0.005 is an unargued guess that ignores multi-agent simultaneous release, which is precisely Esvelt's scenario and the one that breaks the 'survivors are geographically isolated' argument; XPT superforecasters will say even 4e-6/yr is two orders of magnitude too high given that no pathogen in recorded history, including the Black Death and 1918, came near extinction. Do not treat the modelled extinction rate as a consensus figure; it is a derived quantity of a tier decomposition I chose, and the tier probabilities themselves are author-estimates with no published elicitation behind them. Ord's reasoning for 1-in-30 is NOT reproduced here: I could not retrieve the text of Chapter 5 of The Precipice this session, only his headline number via a secondary tabulation (Risk Frontiers) and his own restatement of the number on tobyord.com. Anyone compiling this into a model should read the primary chapter before attributing reasoning to him. Two further retrieval caveats: (1) WebFetch was blocked by a safety classifier partway through this session, so the Esvelt GCSP paper, the XPT PDF, the Global BioLabs 2023 PDF, the Lancet 7-1-7 paper, the RAND report, the Science 2025 paper's numeric results, and the IGSC/NTI/OSTP pages were retrieved as live WebSearch result summaries quoting those sources, not as full texts — the figures are quoted as the summaries stated them and should be spot-checked against the primary documents. The Wittmann et al. counts (76,080 sequences, 72 proteins of concern) came through secondary reporting of the Science paper; the author list, journal and 2 October 2025 date were confirmed on the Microsoft Research publication page directly. The Lancet 7-1-7 first author was not verified. (2) I could not retrieve a primary per-base DNA synthesis cost series this session; search results offered figures ($0.0009/base in 2024, $0.07/base 'currently', ~21%/yr decline) with unclear or non-authoritative provenance, so I have DELIBERATELY OMITTED a cost-per-base parameter rather than dress a poorly-sourced number as a citation. Esvelt's absolute construct costs (US$1,500 / ~US$2,000) are the only synthesis-cost figures here with a clear published source. Finally, the actor-count parameter's current value of 30 is an author-estimate anchored only on the 27 countries hosting BSL-4 labs; no published count of 'actors with capability' exists, and the true value depends entirely on where the capability threshold is drawn.

hazards.name: Accidental release of an enhanced or high-consequence pathogen from a research facility
hazards.oneLine: A pathogen made more dangerous for research purposes, or a high-consequence agent held for study, escapes containment and seeds a human outbreak.
hazards.mechanism: An infected worker, a containment failure or a filtration fault carries a pathogen out of a laboratory; the released organism then behaves exactly as a natural outbreak except that its properties were selected in the laboratory rather than by natural selection. The 1979 Sverdlovsk release demonstrates the physical chain concretely: an aerosol escaped a military microbiology facility, the plume followed the prevailing wind, and casualties fell in a narrow downwind zone. Anthrax is not transmissible person to person, so Sverdlovsk terminated after one generation; the catastrophic branch requires a respiratory-transmissible agent, where the released organism seeds a chain of human transmission that ordinary outbreak response must then race. Deaths in the small tiers are direct infection deaths. In the large tiers, the killing mechanism converges with the deliberate-release hazard: healthcare collapse, then interruption of food, fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains, then famine and untreated ordinary illness. The distinguishing risk-structure feature versus deliberate release is that accident probability scales with the volume of research activity, so it is directly governed by a countable and regulable quantity — laboratories and their oversight regimes — whereas deliberate release scales with intent, which is not countable.

The abstract confirms the five-substitution count: 'Four amino acid substitutions in the host receptor-binding protein hemagglutinin, and one in the polymerase complex protein basic polymerase 2, were consistently present in airborne-transmitted viruses' and 'None of the recipient ferrets died after airborne infection'. THE 'ALL OF WHICH HAD BEEN OBSERVED INDIVIDUALLY IN WILD VIRUSES' CLAIM IS WRONG. The packet's own companion source (CIDRAP, cite 4) says only that 'two of the mutations involved (T156A and E627K) are common in natural H5N1 isolates', with E627K in ~27% of avian and ~29% of human H5N1 sequences. This matters for the packet's model: the whole point of the H5N1 episode as an information hazard is that the specific COMBINATION, not each individual substitution, was the novel and hazardous result. Also, the NSABB's recommendation against full publication was announced in DECEMBER 2011, not 'autumn 2011'.

hazards.uncertainty: THE ANNUAL PROBABILITY HERE IS AN AUTHOR-ESTIMATE AND IS THE WEAKEST NUMBER IN THIS PACKET. I retrieved exactly one documented accidental release with quantified human casualties this session (Sverdlovsk 1979). The well-known published per-lab-year escape estimates — Lipsitch and Inglesby's analysis accompanying the 2014 US gain-of-function funding pause, and Klotz's laboratory-acquired-infection frequency work — I was NOT able to retrieve this session (the WebSearch budget was exhausted and WebFetch was blocked by a safety classifier), so I have not cited them and have not used their numbers. My 0.02/yr central value is a judgement built from one verified event plus the widely reported but unverified-this-session cluster of laboratory-associated outbreaks (1978 Birmingham smallpox, the 2003-04 SARS laboratory escapes); a reviewer should replace it with a properly sourced per-lab-year figure before the model is used for anything decision-relevant. The derived per-lab-year escape probability of ~3e-4 is therefore also unsourced. Two further weaknesses. First, the denominator is wrong in a known direction: I have scaled on BSL-4 labs because that is the number Global BioLabs counts, but work on transmissible respiratory pathogens largely occurs at BSL-3/BSL-3+, which is far more numerous and much less well enumerated, so the model understates the exposed base and correspondingly overstates the per-lab hazard. Second, the top two severity tiers are extrapolations with no empirical anchor whatsoever: no accidental release in history has produced a global pandemic with agreed attribution, and the one candidate event that is publicly contested (SARS-CoV-2 origins) I deliberately excluded because its attribution is unresolved and including a contested case would smuggle a disputed prior into the tier weights. A critic will reasonably say that excluding it biases the top tiers low. On the H5N1 citation: note the important qualifier that the airborne-transmissible ferret virus was reported as not lethal by the airborne route, so the experiments are evidence about the information hazard and about transmissibility enhancement, NOT evidence that a transmissible-and-lethal agent was produced; conflating those two is the standard error in commentary on this episode.

hazards.name: Large-scale state biological weapons programme use
hazards.oneLine: A state with an industrial-scale biological weapons programme uses it in conflict, at the production scale historically demonstrated by the Soviet Union.
hazards.mechanism: State programmes differ from non-state attempts by orders of magnitude in three respects that all bear directly on the death toll: production scale, delivery engineering, and the ability to select and characterise agents against defined military requirements. The Soviet programme is the only case with reliable public figures on scale, and it establishes that the industrial capability existed at the level of hundreds of tons of formulated agent and tens of thousands of staff. Use in conflict kills initially through mass exposure of a target population; the catastrophic branch arises only if a transmissible agent is used, at which point the attacker loses control of the outcome and the agent returns through the same travel networks. From there the mechanism is identical to the other two hazards: healthcare collapse, then breakdown of the food, fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains, then famine. A state programme is also the only actor class plausibly able to mount a simultaneous multi-agent release, which is the scenario in which the geographic-isolation argument against extinction fails. Note the counterweight the historical record provides: the Soviet programme was never used, and its most significant human toll was a domestic accident.

rate.eventDefinition: deliberate state use of biological weapons in armed conflict causing 100,000 or more deaths
rate.trend: Unclear. The BWC entered into force in 1975 and the Soviet programme was dismantled after 1992, so declared state programmes have fallen; against that, Ord's 2023 revisit notes nuclear risk is up, and the same great-power tensions that drive it would drive any renewed programme. I could not retrieve the current US State Department arms control compliance assessment this session, so the number of states currently assessed as having offensive programmes is UNKNOWN in this packet.

rateMods.why: use happens inside armed conflict, so it scales with the tempo of confrontation
weakly rising: state programmes are gated on political decision more than on technical capability

tiers.split: theatre-scale, ~90% prompt

hazards.uncertainty: BOTH THE ANNUAL PROBABILITY AND THE CURRENT VALUE OF THE state_programmes KNOB ARE AUTHOR-ESTIMATES WITH NO SOURCE RETRIEVED THIS SESSION. I attempted to retrieve the current US State Department Arms Control Compliance Report — the standard public document that names states assessed as maintaining offensive biological weapons programmes in violation of the BWC — and the WebSearch budget was exhausted before that search executed. The value of 3 is therefore a placeholder reflecting my prior that a small number of states are publicly assessed as non-compliant; IT SHOULD BE REPLACED WITH THE COMPLIANCE REPORT'S ACTUAL ASSESSMENT BEFORE USE, and a reviewer should treat any conclusion that depends on it as unsupported. Likewise the 0.001/yr base rate has no elicitation behind it: the historical record contains zero instances of large-scale state biological weapons use in the eighty years since the technology matured, which by a naive Laplace rule of succession over ~80 programme-rich years gives an upper bound nearer 1e-2/yr and a point estimate that could reasonably be an order of magnitude below my figure. A critic can attack this from either side and I cannot defend the specific value. The severity tiers are also unanchored: no state has used biological weapons at scale, so unlike the deliberate-release hazard (where the XPT and Ord give at least two independent elicitations) there is nothing here but my judgement. What IS well-sourced in this entry is the programme-scale data — Alibek's figures are first-hand congressional testimony, corroborated on personnel and facility counts by the independent University of Kent account, and they establish the demonstrated industrial ceiling. Use this hazard entry for its scale parameters and its structural role (state programmes as the only actor class capable of multi-agent strategic release, and as the upstream source of both expertise leakage and containment accidents), NOT for its probability. One further caveat on the Alibek testimony: it is a single defector's account given in a policy setting sixteen years after the events described, and some of his specific claims have been disputed in the arms-control literature; the personnel and facility figures are the best-corroborated part of it and the tonnage figures the least.

hazards.name: Regional nuclear exchange (India–Pakistan class, 100–500 urban detonations)
hazards.oneLine: Two regional nuclear powers detonate on the order of 100–500 warheads on each other's cities, and the resulting urban firestorms loft enough soot into the stratosphere to collapse global crop yields for roughly a decade.
hazards.mechanism: The chain is: fire → fuel → soot → stratosphere → sunlight → calories → famine. (1) A 15-kt airburst ignites everything inside a fire zone taken by Toon et al. 2019 as equal to Hiroshima's, 13 km², with the ignition area scaling proportionally to yield. (2) Toon et al. allocate 11,000 kg of flammable material per person in the burned area from a gridded population database — about 4 g/cm² for a dense modern city (WWII Hamburg measurements span 12–47 g/cm²; sparse 1990 San Jose is 1.34 g/cm²). (3) The mass fire consumes that fuel at an adopted black-carbon emission factor of 0.02 g BC per g fuel burned. (4) Fire convection injects the smoke into the 300–150 hPa layer (~9–13.5 km); Toon et al. assume 20% is rained out at injection and 10–15% more in the first few days, so 30–35% is lost before the stratosphere. What survives is self-lofted higher by solar heating of the black carbon into a layer with no precipitation removal, giving an e-folding lifetime of ~4.6 years in the Robock et al. 2007 model. (5) A 250-weapon/100-kt exchange yields 37 Tg of soot and about 5.5 °C of global cooling; Toon et al. 2019's regional case cuts surface sunlight 20–35%, cools the surface 2–5 °C and cuts precipitation 15–30%, with recovery taking more than 10 years. (6) Xia et al. 2022 pushed those climate fields through crop and fishery models: total calories available from the major staple crops and wild marine fisheries fall 23% at 16 Tg, 33% at 27 Tg, 42% at 37 Tg and 48% at 47 Tg, hitting hardest at mid-to-high northern latitudes — Canada, the USA, Europe, Russia, China, the world's grain belt. (7) They then counted, nation by nation, how many people fall persistently below a 1,911 kcal/person/day starvation cutoff after livestock are slaughtered, animal feed is diverted to humans, household waste is eliminated and international food trade is halted. What actually kills people is therefore neither blast nor fire nor fallout: it is the loss of the traded calorie surplus in food-importing and high-latitude countries thousands of kilometres from the war. Xia et al.'s model shows zero famine deaths in India and Pakistan in the smaller scenarios precisely because it counts only climate-driven crop loss, not the war zone itself.

rate.eventDefinition: A nuclear exchange between two states in which at least ~100 warheads of ≥15 kt are detonated on urban/industrial targets, injecting ≥5 Tg of soot into the stratosphere — Xia et al. 2022's threshold above which mass food shortages occur in almost all countries. NOT the probability of any nuclear detonation, and NOT the probability of the famine outcome.
rate.trend: Rising. Toon et al. 2019 project India and Pakistan at 400–500 warheads by 2025 with yields running from tested 12–45 kt values up to a few hundred kilotons, against ~130–150 each in 2018; FAS put India at 190 and Pakistan at 170 warheads at the beginning of 2026. Bigger, higher-yield arsenals move the same exchange up the soot curve even if the rate of exchanges is flat: 250 weapons at 15 kt gives 16 Tg, the same 250 at 100 kt gives 37 Tg. Urban populations in the two countries were projected to grow ~90% between 2000 and 2025, raising the fuel load per target.

only weakly rising in the GLOBAL count: a regional exchange is driven by its own dyad, not by the world total

sevMods.why: soot is roughly linear in the fraction of warheads landing on cities up to target-list exhaustion, and Xia et al.'s famine deaths follow soot directly. This is the single most decisive severity knob on the board

Recovery of the climate takes about a decade; the political and trade order does not necessarily recover.

hazards.uncertainty:
WEAKEST LINK — provenance of the scenario table. The Nature Food paper itself is paywalled (nature.com returns an IdP redirect; the UTRGV repository copy returns HTTP 403). The per-scenario Tg/direct-fatality/famine-death table I report was read directly from the IPPNW "Nuclear Famine" 2022 PDF, whose Table 1 is captioned "adapted from Xia et al, Nature Food, August 2022" and whose Table 2 is captioned "Adapted from Toon et al 2007, Toon et al 2019, and Xia et al 2022." It is therefore a faithful secondary source, not the primary table. It cross-checks against the NASA GISS abstract of Xia et al. (">2 billion" India–Pakistan versus my 2,675.3 million at 47 Tg; ">5 billion" US–Russia versus 5,413 million at 150 Tg) and against Toon et al. 2019's own "16 to 36 Tg" and "50 to 125 million" ranges, which I read from the primary PDF. An auditor should replace the table with the primary Nature Food figures before this is used in anger. Note also a genuine tension I did not resolve: Toon et al. 2019's abstract says 16–36 Tg for the 250-weapon family, while the Xia scenario set runs to 47 Tg for 500 weapons — the 47 Tg case is the larger scenario, not a contradiction, but the 36-vs-37 Tg discrepancy for 250×100 kt is unexplained rounding I could not check.

SECOND WEAKNESS — the annual probability. There is no published per-year rate for the event as I have defined it (≥100 urban warheads, ≥5 Tg). The XPT numbers are for the OUTCOME (>10% of humanity dead within 5 years), which at 5 Tg is not reached (5.4%), so the XPT figures under-count 5 Tg exchanges and I have set my best estimate above the annualised XPT expert figure (8% by 2100 over 78 years = 1.07e-3/yr) and my low bound below the superforecaster figure (4% = 5.2e-4/yr). The high bound of 5e-3/yr is roughly five times the expert annualisation and is my own judgement, not a published number. A serious critic would attack (a) treating a cumulative-to-2100 elicitation as a constant Poisson rate when forecasters plainly expect the rate to change, and (b) using superforecaster medians at all, given that no one has a track record on 78-year questions.

THIRD — the soot exponents. The Tg ≈ 16 × (N/250)^0.35 × (Y/15)^0.45 fit is MINE, fitted to four published points. It reproduces those four exactly but has no independent validation and it does NOT extrapolate to the 100×15 kt = 5 Tg "prequel" case, which comes from the older Toon/Robock 2007 emission model with smaller cities and lower fuel loads (my formula would give 11.6 Tg there). Do not use it below 250 weapons.

FOURTH — the physics that everyone actually fights about. Whether urban mass fires loft smoke into the stratosphere at all is contested. Toon et al. 2019 respond to a Los Alamos study (Reisner et al.) arguing the smoke would not reach the stratosphere, and rebut it on the ground that it simulated a detonation over sparse suburban Atlanta at 1.07 g/cm² fuel loading, about an order of magnitude below even the least dense target considered. The observational support is indirect: 2017 British Columbia and 2019–2020 Australian wildfire pyrocumulonimbus were tracked lofting to 12 km and then self-lofting to 23 km over two months. That is a few tenths of a teragram, three orders of magnitude below the scenarios. The rainout fraction (30–35%), the BC emission factor (0.02 g/g), the 11,000 kg/person fuel allocation and the assumption that essentially all fuel in the ignition zone burns are each single-figure parameters carrying at least a factor-of-two uncertainty, and they multiply.

FIFTH — what the Xia model deliberately omits, all of which push deaths UP: radioactive fallout, ozone loss and UV damage to crops, breakdown of fuel/fertiliser/seed supply chains, epidemic disease, and the collapse of public order. It also omits the possibility that trade does NOT halt, which pushes deaths down. Xia et al. themselves note that during the 1943 Bengal famine a 5% drop in available food produced 3 million deaths through hoarding and price inflation — i.e. the mapping from calorie availability to deaths is not the smooth cutoff the model assumes.

SIXTH — the death tolls are computed against a 2010 world population of 6,703 million. Absolute counts scale up by roughly 1.2× for a present-day population; I have reported FRACTIONS to keep the model internally consistent. The tolls are also "by the end of year two," not year ten, so they are a lower bound on the ten-year figure the schema asks for.

hazards.name: Full-scale strategic nuclear exchange (United States–Russia)
hazards.oneLine: The deployed US and Russian strategic arsenals are used against each other's cities and industry, injecting roughly 150 Tg of soot and producing years of below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers.
hazards.mechanism: Physically the same chain as the regional case, but two orders of magnitude further along it. (1) Toon et al. 2008, as reported in Toon et al. 2019, computed 180 Tg of black carbon from 4,400 detonations of 100 kt on urban areas — roughly half the combined arsenals of the USA, Russia, China, Britain and France — at a yield lower than the average. Note the per-weapon soot is only 0.041 Tg, versus 0.148 Tg per weapon for the 250 densest Indian/Pakistani targets: the target list is exhausted, so soot saturates hard. (2) Robock et al. 2007 used 150 Tg of smoke as the superpower-war injection and found an e-folding stratospheric lifetime of 4.6 years, because black carbon absorbs sunlight, heats the surrounding air, and self-lofts above any precipitation removal. (3) Coupe et al. 2019 re-ran 150 Tg of black carbon injected into the 150–300 mb layer in WACCM4 at 2° resolution with 66 levels to 140 km, with full stratospheric chemistry and fractal particle growth, and compared it against the older GISS ModelE run: both produce a true nuclear winter, with global average surface temperatures plummeting by more than 8 K and below-freezing temperatures over much of the Northern Hemisphere during summer. The higher-resolution model removes smoke faster through particle growth but produces LARGER temperature and precipitation reductions in the first few years, so the aerosol-microphysics refinement did not rescue the result. (4) With sunlight cut, mid-latitude grain-growing regions are held below freezing through what should be the growing season and agriculture in the Northern Hemisphere simply stops. (5) Xia et al. 2022 carried the 150 Tg fields through crop and fishery models and, applying a 1,911 kcal/person/day starvation cutoff nation by nation after livestock slaughter, feed diversion and the halt of international food trade, found 5,413 million dead by the end of year two out of a modelled world population of 6,703 million — 80.8%. The United States loses 309.6 million of 312.2 million, China 1,362 of 1,367, Russia 142 of 143.6. Again, almost none of these deaths are from blast, fire or fallout; they are from the loss of a growing season, repeated, in every food-producing latitude at once.

rate.eventDefinition: A nuclear exchange between the United States and Russia in which a substantial fraction of the deployed strategic arsenals is used, including against urban and industrial targets — i.e. an exchange large enough to put ≳50 Tg of soot into the stratosphere. This is the probability the WAR OCCURS, not the probability it kills most of humanity (see severity tiers) and not the probability it ends humanity (see below).
rate.trend: Rising, modestly. FAS put the world at ~12,187 warheads and nine nuclear states at the beginning of 2026, with dismantlement slowing and new deployments accelerating, and China's stockpile at ~620 and growing — turning a two-body strategic problem into a three-body one. Barrett et al.'s own caution cuts the other way: their false-alarm rate data are from 1977–1983 and NORAD has not released false-alarm rates since the mid-1980s, so a real decline in the underlying rate would not be visible in their model.

rateMods.why: Hellman: ~6% per year of a potential initiating event, times ~1/3 that it becomes a full crisis
a larger arsenal raises both the chance a crisis goes strategic and the number of hands on a launch decision, but sub-linearly — the 1986 peak of ~70,300 was not six times more dangerous than today

sevMods.why: Toon et al.: soot scales with cities burned, and it is soot that starves people. A purely counterforce exchange is a fraction as lethal globally as a countervalue one with the same warheads
severe diminishing returns once the target list is exhausted — Toon et al. 2008's 180 Tg came from far more warheads than exist today, and halving the arsenal does not halve the soot

tiers.label: Counterforce-weighted exchange
tiers.desc: Missile fields, submarine bases, bomber bases and command nodes are hit but cities are largely spared, so urban fuel loads are not consumed and stratospheric soot stays well below the 150 Tg case. Direct deaths are in the tens to low hundreds of millions from blast and fallout over silo fields and their downwind populations; the famine chain fires only weakly. Industrial and agricultural capacity in both belligerents is nonetheless wrecked.
tiers.split: counterforce-weighted: relatively more of the deaths are prompt because relatively less soot goes up

tiers.label: Full countervalue exchange — 150 Tg nuclear winter
tiers.desc: Xia et al. 2022 scenario 5. 150 Tg of soot, global mean surface cooling of more than 8 K (Coupe et al. 2019), below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers for years. 5,413 million dead by the end of year two out of 6,703 million — 80.8% — overwhelmingly from famine, and overwhelmingly outside the belligerent states. Recovery of the climate takes over a decade; recovery of industrial capacity is the binding constraint and is not modelled by anyone.
tiers.split: Xia et al. 150 Tg: ~360M direct against >5bn without adequate calories. 5.5% of this toll is prompt. This tier is the single best-sourced catastrophe on the whole board and it is 94% a famine

tiers.label: Winter plus civilisational collapse
tiers.desc: The 150 Tg climate outcome compounded by what Xia et al. explicitly exclude: fallout, 25%+ global ozone loss and UV damage to what crops remain, breakdown of fuel, fertiliser, seed and medicine supply chains, epidemic disease among a starving population, and the collapse of public order and of any coordinated response. Survivors are scattered, pre-industrial and concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere — Australia, New Zealand, southern South America and southern Africa show the smallest modelled losses. Industrial civilisation has to be rebuilt from a depleted resource base.
tiers.split: winter plus civilisational collapse

tiers.label: Terminal
tiers.desc: No recovery: the surviving population falls below a viable threshold, or survives without ever rebuilding. NOTE that Xia et al. do not claim this and no climate model produces it — this tier exists only because Ord and the XPT forecasters assign it non-zero probability, and because Barrett et al. open their paper by citing the possibility of "collapse of modern civilization worldwide, and even the extinction of humanity." The conditional probability here is derived, not published: Ord's 1-in-1,000 existential risk from nuclear war over the next century, divided by a roughly 10% chance of a full-scale exchange in that century, gives ~1% conditional.
tiers.split: the tail

cascades.why: this is the actual killing mechanism and it is already internal to the tier figures; the boost is for what a SECOND shock does on top
loss of grids, refining and Haber-Bosch
ammonia synthesis needs an intact industrial base; roughly half the world is fed by it
undernutrition raises infectious-disease incidence and case-fatality
the post-war order

citations.claim: Annual probability of inadvertent US–Russia nuclear war from misinterpretation of early-warning false alarms, with the full uncertainty range.
citations.authors: Anthony M. Barrett, Seth D. Baum, Kelly R. Hostetler (Global Catastrophic Risk Institute)
citations.figure: Median model-estimated annual inadvertence probability, status quo: 0.009 under "Danger Calm" base-case assumptions and 0.003 under the "Safe Calm" sensitivity case (Tables 3 and 4). "The 90 percent confidence interval (extending from the 5th percentile to the 95th percentile model estimate) ranges from 0.0002 to 0.07 in the base case, and from 0.00001 to 0.05 if excluding launch during low tensions." Median annual rate of mistaken MAC-level attack indications: 0.01 from usual false alarms and 0.0006 from nuclear terrorist attack (Danger Calm); 0.003 and 0.0000008 (Safe Calm). Empirical ceiling: given 37 event-free years 1975–2012, "there could be a statistical argument for rejecting (with 95 percent confidence) a probabilistic model that produced a best estimate … for annual nuclear war probability above 0.08." They also report Hellman's independent estimate that "the failure rate of [U.S.–Russia nuclear war] deterrence from all sources is on the order of one percent per year," which they note "is approximately equivalent to this article's Danger Calm median estimated annual probability."

citations.claim: A 150 Tg soot injection from a US–Russia war produces a true nuclear winter, with more than 8 K of global mean surface cooling and below-freezing Northern Hemisphere summers.
citations.authors: Joshua Coupe, Charles G. Bardeen, Alan Robock, Owen B. Toon
citations.venue: Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres 124: 8522–8543, DOI 10.1029/2019JD030509
citations.figure: "Current nuclear arsenals used in a war between the United States and Russia could inject 150 Tg of soot from fires ignited by nuclear explosions into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere." Key point: "A true nuclear winter occurs in both models as black carbon aerosols block sunlight and cause global average surface temperatures to plummet by more than 8 K." "Nuclear winter, with below freezing temperatures over much of the Northern Hemisphere during summer, occurs because of a reduction of surface solar radiation due to smoke lofted into the stratosphere." "WACCM4's more sophisticated aerosol representation removes smoke more quickly, but the magnitude of the climate response is not reduced. In fact, the higher-resolution WACCM4 simulates larger temperature and precipitation reductions than ModelE in the first few years." Also reports that Robock, Oman & Stenchikov (2007) "found an e-folding lifetime of 4.6 years for soot particles in the stratosphere."

citations.claim: The soot-to-famine conversion for the 150 Tg US–Russia scenario, and the physical soot-emission chain that produces the 150–180 Tg figure.
citations.authors: Matt Bivens (IPPNW), tables adapted from Xia et al. 2022 Nature Food and Toon et al. 2007/2019; soot-emission parameters from Toon et al. 2019 Science Advances
citations.venue: IPPNW "Nuclear Famine" report; Toon et al., Science Advances 5(10): eaay5478
citations.figure: IPPNW Table 2, scenario 5 ("A global nuclear war generates 150 Tg of soot, with years of below-freezing temperatures in summers"): 5,413 million dead worldwide by end of year two, out of a 2010 world population of 6,703 million. Per-nation: United States 309.6 of 312.2; China 1,362.3 of 1,367.4; Russia 142 of 143.6; India 731.1 of 1,205.6; Japan 125.6 of 127.4; Germany 82.9 of 83; UK 62.2 of 62.3; Australia 0 of 22.4. Toon et al. 2019 report that "Toon et al. estimated that 180 Tg (1 Tg = 10^12 g) of black carbon (BC) could be generated by a total of 4400 explosions of 100-kt weapons in urban areas, about half the arsenals of Russia, China, Britain, France, and the United States." Emission parameters: 13 km² fire zone for a 15-kt airburst (Hiroshima), scaling proportional to yield; "11,000 kg of flammable material" allocated per person in the burned area; "we use an average BC (or soot) emission factor for burned fuel based on studies summarized by Turco et al., yielding 0.02 g BC/g fuel burned"; injection into the 300- to 150-hPa layer (~9 to ~13.5 km); "we assume that 20% of the BC is removed by rainfall during injection into the upper troposphere… in total, 30 to 35% of the smoke is removed by rainfall before it enters the stratosphere."
