citations.claim: Existential (permanent, terminal) risk from nuclear war over the next century — a different quantity from the probability of the war or of mass death.
citations.authors: Toby Ord
citations.venue: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity, Bloomsbury (Table 6.1); as restated by the author in "The Precipice Revisited"
citations.figure: "1 in 1,000" chance of an existential catastrophe from nuclear war in the next 100 years. Ord notes his estimates were "rounded off (usually to the nearest factor of 10)" and, in the revisit, says only "Nuclear is up" without giving a revised number.

citations.claim: The historical near-miss record exists but has deliberately NOT been converted into a probability by the researchers who assembled it.
citations.authors: Seth D. Baum, Robert de Neufville, Anthony M. Barrett
citations.venue: Global Catastrophic Risk Institute Working Paper 18-1, "A Model For The Probability Of Nuclear War"
citations.figure: "60 historical incidents are included, making this perhaps the largest such dataset currently available" spanning 1945 to ~2015 (including World War II itself), across 14 interrelated scenarios. Labelled incidents in their Figure 1 include the Cuban Missile Crisis, the B-59 (Arkhipov) incident, Able Archer, Petrov, the Norwegian Rocket Incident, Goldsboro, Thule, Damascus, the Florida Satellite Incident, BMEWS, Penkovsky, the SAC Chip Failure and the Hawaii Alert. Critically: "the paper stops short of attempting to estimate these probabilities. At this stage of the research, estimating the probabilities would require considerable guesswork and is likely to be quite mistaken." And: "the 'closeness' of the events is a matter of subtle historical interpretation, something that experts in the field disagree on" — citing Lewis et al. (2014) that many incidents came quite close, against Tertrais (2017) that no incident since WWII has come close.

citations.claim: Independent expert and superforecaster elicitations of nuclear catastrophe and nuclear extinction probability, which bound the terminal tier.
citations.authors: Forecasting Research Institute (Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament)
citations.venue: Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT), figures via EA Forum analysis of the FRI report
citations.figure: Nuclear catastrophe (>10% of humans dead within 5 years) by 2100: superforecasters 4%, domain experts 8%. Nuclear extinction (world population below 5,000) by 2100: superforecasters 0.074%, domain experts 0.55%. Nuclear weapon use killing >1,000 in a single event by 2030: superforecasters 4%, domain experts 4.5%.

hazards.uncertainty:
THE THREE PROBABILITIES ARE DIFFERENT AND I HAVE KEPT THEM APART. (a) P(event) — a full-scale US–Russia exchange occurs — is my 1e-3/yr best estimate, range 1e-4 to 9e-3. (b) P(kills a large fraction | event) is in severity_tiers: 60% for the 150 Tg/80.8% mortality outcome, i.e. P ≈ 6e-4/yr unconditionally. (c) P(permanent end of humanity | event) is 1%, i.e. ~1e-5/yr, which over a century is ~1e-3 and is exactly Ord's 1-in-1,000. That agreement is not independent evidence — I derived the conditional FROM Ord's number, so it is circular by construction and must not be read as a cross-check.

THE PROBABILITY IS THE WEAKEST FIGURE HERE. My best estimate of 1e-3/yr sits an order of magnitude BELOW Barrett et al.'s Danger Calm median of 0.009/yr. That is deliberate and it is an author judgement, not a published position: Barrett et al. estimate the probability of INADVERTENT LAUNCH in response to mistaken attack indications, which is a broader event than a full-scale countervalue exchange (a launch could be limited, or aborted, or answered in kind at a lower level), and their false-alarm rates come from 1977–1983 US data, a six-year sample from the sharpest period of the late Cold War, applied unchanged to 1975–2012. They say so themselves: NORAD has not released false-alarm rates since the mid-1980s, so they cannot tell whether the rate fell. Against that, they note their own model cannot be rejected at 95% confidence given 37 event-free years unless its mean exceeds 0.08. My high bound of 9e-3 is exactly their Danger Calm median; my low bound of 1e-4 sits between their two 5th-percentiles and Hellman's Cuba-only lower bound of 2e-4. A serious critic will attack the whole exercise: 81 years with zero events cannot distinguish 1e-2 from 1e-4, and the Baum/de Neufville/Barrett team who assembled the largest near-miss dataset (60 incidents) explicitly refused to convert it into a rate because "the 'closeness' of the events is a matter of subtle historical interpretation, something that experts in the field disagree on" — Lewis et al. 2014 say many came close, Tertrais 2017 says none did. That refusal is the most honest position in the literature and my number does not have its authority.

SCENARIO-TABLE PROVENANCE. As with the regional hazard, the 150 Tg death toll of 5,413 million was read from IPPNW's Table 2, captioned as adapted from Xia et al. 2022 and Toon et al. 2007/2019, because the Nature Food primary is paywalled and the repository copy returns 403. It cross-checks against the NASA GISS abstract's "more than 5 billion could die from a war between the United States and Russia." I could NOT retrieve a direct-fatality figure for the 150 Tg scenario — IPPNW's Table 1 gives direct fatalities only for the five regional cases — so the deaths_fraction of 0.808 for the winter tier is famine deaths ALONE and excludes prompt blast/fire/fallout deaths in the USA and Russia. It is therefore an underestimate, and I have not attempted to fill the gap with a number I did not retrieve.

SOOT SATURATION IS THE UNDER-APPRECIATED PHYSICS. The per-weapon soot yield falls from 0.148 Tg (top 250 South Asian targets) to 0.041 Tg (4,400 global urban targets) because the world's dense cities run out. Any simulator that makes soot linear in warhead count will badly overstate the marginal effect of the last few thousand warheads and badly understate the effect of the first few hundred. Conversely the 47 Tg regional case already kills 42% of humanity, so the marginal humanitarian value of arms reductions from 12,000 to, say, 1,000 warheads is much smaller than the weapon count suggests — a conclusion an arms-control advocate would dislike but which follows directly from Toon et al.'s own numbers.

WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE WHOLE CHAIN. The famine result rests on urban firestorms lofting soot to the stratosphere. That has never been observed at scale. The observational analogues are 2017 British Columbia and 2019–2020 Australian wildfire pyroCb, which lofted a few tenths of a teragram to 12 km and then self-lofted to 23 km over two months — the right physics, three orders of magnitude short of the required mass, and forest rather than city fuel. If real urban fires under nuclear attack produce conflagrations rather than firestorms, burn a much smaller fraction of the available fuel because it is buried under rubble (Toon et al. concede perhaps 20% or more could be effectively buried in the high-overpressure zone), or fail to generate the convective column, the entire mechanism collapses and this hazard reduces to a regional catastrophe with a global economic depression. That is the Los Alamos position, and it is not obviously wrong — it is merely, in Toon et al.'s rebuttal, based on an unrepresentative sparse-suburban simulation.

hazards.name: Non-nuclear great-power and interstate war
hazards.oneLine: Conventional war between states follows a fat-tailed severity distribution with no detectable downward trend in severity, so a war far larger than any yet fought is a live possibility even though the last eighty years have been quiet.
hazards.mechanism: A dispute between great powers escalates to open war; industrial mobilisation converts national economies into war production and the fighting continues until one side's capacity to resist collapses. Direct combat deaths are only part of the toll: the dominant killers in every historically large war have been famine, displacement and epidemic disease following the destruction of agriculture, transport and sanitation — the Thirty Years' War, the Taiping Rebellion, the An Lushan rebellion and the Eastern Front of WWII all killed far more civilians through starvation and disease than through weapons. A modern global war would additionally sever the container-shipping, fertiliser (Haber-Bosch nitrogen), fuel and pharmaceutical supply chains on which roughly half of current food production and nearly all urban populations depend, so the mass-death mechanism is regional famine and infrastructure loss in food-importing countries, not battlefield casualties. Critically, no observed or plausible conventional war reaches human extinction: even the largest tail events in the historical record kill single-digit percentages of humanity, and Cirillo and Taleb argue explicitly that the true mean of the casualty distribution is bounded by world population and cannot be infinite. The hazard here is civilisational damage and the cascade into worse hazards, not termination.

rate.eventDefinition: onset of an armed conflict killing at least 1,000,000 people (combatants and civilians, direct violence), excluding any use of nuclear weapons
rate.trend: Genuinely contested and the single most important open question in this hazard. Cirillo & Taleb (2016) test the 1500-2015 window and cannot reject a homogeneous Poisson process (504 events; no significant trend, season or temporal dependence over the entire time window), i.e. FLAT. Clauset (2018) likewise finds war onsets consistent with a stationary geometric process 1823-2003 and finds the post-1940 distribution of war sizes not statistically distinguishable from 1823-1939, i.e. FLAT. Spagat & Thompson (2026, ISQ) reach the opposite conclusion for a narrower quantity — the ONSET FREQUENCY of Western European great-power wars — reporting a sustained decline (annualised onset rate 0.27/yr in 1495-1599 falling to 0.040/yr in 1900-2024, with zero great-power wars since 1953, max p = 0.002 across 401 breakpoint tests). These are not necessarily contradictory: Spagat & Thompson measure how OFTEN great powers in one region start wars; Clauset and Cirillo & Taleb measure how BIG wars are globally and whether the size distribution has shifted. A declining onset rate combined with an unchanged fat-tailed severity distribution is coherent. For a simulator, treat frequency as plausibly declining and severity-given-occurrence as flat.

rateMods.why: Cirillo & Taleb and Clauset independently find war severity extremely fat-tailed and the 'long peace' not statistically distinguishable from chance, so the base rate is treated as stationary and only the crisis tempo moves it

tiers.label: Major regional war
tiers.desc: 1-10 million dead, comparable to the Korean War, the Iran-Iraq War or the Second Congo War. Regional famine and displacement; global industrial capacity essentially untouched.
tiers.split: 70% prompt: war kills by violence, but war famine and disease have historically been comparable

tiers.label: World-war scale
tiers.desc: 10-100 million dead, comparable to WWI or WWII (Clauset records WWII at 16,634,907 battle deaths; Cirillo & Taleb estimate ~73 million total victims). Multi-continent mobilisation, sustained famine in occupied and blockaded regions, decade-scale reconstruction.
tiers.split: world-war scale

tiers.label: Beyond any recorded war
tiers.desc: 100 million to 1 billion dead. No historical precedent in absolute numbers. Collapse of global trade in food, fuel and fertiliser causes famine well outside the belligerent states; the deaths are overwhelmingly in food-importing countries not party to the war.
tiers.split: beyond any recorded war — the fat tail Cirillo & Taleb argue is under-appreciated

tiers.label: Civilisational
tiers.desc: Over 1 billion dead. Requires either the fat tail delivering an event several orders of magnitude beyond the record, or the conflict cascading into nuclear, biological or infrastructural collapse. Industrial civilisation is set back but the physical and knowledge base for recovery survives; even Cirillo & Taleb's infinite-apparent-mean tail is bounded by world population.
tiers.split: civilisational

cascades.why: conventional great-power war is the dominant pathway to nuclear use — gated on the world-war-scale tiers and above, because most conflicts killing a million people involve no nuclear-armed state at all and an ungated cascade inflated the nuclear hazard by nearly a factor of two

same — gated on the world-war-scale tiers and above, because most conflicts killing a million people involve no nuclear-armed state at all and an ungated cascade inflated the nuclear hazard by nearly a factor of two
essentially all chemical-weapons deaths since 1918 occurred inside wars

use requires a war to use them in — gated on the world-war-scale tiers and above, because most conflicts killing a million people involve no nuclear-armed state at all and an ungated cascade inflated the nuclear hazard by nearly a factor of two
wartime states relax biosafety and restart programmes
a decisive hegemonic victory collapses the number of independent great powers, which is the strongest driver in Caplan's treatment

citations.claim: War casualties are extremely fat-tailed: the GPD shape parameter exceeds 1 in all fits, implying the apparent mean of the distribution does not exist; and the naive sample mean severely understates the true (shadow) mean.
citations.authors: Pasquale Cirillo, Nassim Nicholas Taleb
citations.venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 452:29-45 (arXiv:1505.04722v2 preprint read this session)
citations.figure: Dataset: 565 events over the period 1-2015 AD, all with more than 3000 casualties; 331 conflicts above the 25k threshold (58.6%). Maximum-likelihood GPD shape parameter xi = 1.4985 (SE 0.1233) for raw data at threshold 25k; xi = 1.5868 (SE 0.1265) for rescaled data at 145k; xi = 1.5915 (SE 0.1268) for dual data at 145k. Restricting to 1500-2015 (504 events): xi = 1.4093 raw, 1.4653 rescaled. Conditional shadow mean at the 145k threshold = 3.6885e7 vs conditional sample mean 1.7710e7, ratio 2.08 (ratios range 1.85 to 2.88 over thresholds 50k-1000k). Shadow standard deviation 3.0788e8 vs sample 1.0120e8, ratio 3.04.

citations.claim: The 'long peace' is not statistically distinguishable from chance: large armed conflicts follow a homogeneous Poisson process with no trend over the last 500 years, and the inter-arrival times are far longer than the length of the peace.
citations.authors: Pasquale Cirillo, Nassim Nicholas Taleb
citations.venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 452:29-45 (arXiv:1505.04722v2 preprint read this session)
citations.figure: Average inter-arrival times (raw data, years) with mean absolute deviation: >=0.5M casualties 23.71 (MAD 35.20); >=1M 34.08 (47.73); >=2M 56.44 (72.84); >=5M 93.03 (113.57); >=10M 133.08 (136.88); >=20M 247.14 (261.31); >=50M 345.50 (325.50). Rescaled to 2015 population: >=1M 13.28 (20.53); >=5M 34.88 (46.85); >=10M 52.23 (63.91); >=50M 103.97 (114.25). Verbatim: 'the absence of a conflict generating more than, say, 5 million casualties in the last sixty years is highly insufficient to state that their probability has decreased over time, given that the average inter-arrival time is 93.03 years, with a mean absolute deviation of 113.57 years!' Over 1500-2015, 504 events cannot reject an equiprobable Multinomial distribution at the 10% confidence level.

citations.claim: Interstate war sizes follow a power law and the long peace falls comfortably within the fluctuations of a stationary conflict-generating process; it would have to persist another century or more to become a statistically significant trend.
citations.authors: Aaron Clauset
citations.venue: Science Advances 4(2):eaao3580 (author preprint PDF read this session; PubMed 29507877, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aao3580)
citations.figure: Correlates of War: 95 interstate wars, 1823-2003, battle deaths ranging from 1,000 to 16,634,907 (WWII). Maximum-likelihood power law alpha-hat = 1.53 +/- 0.07 for x >= x_min-hat = 7061, 95% of the bootstrap distribution within [1.37, 1.76], Monte Carlo p_KS = 0.78 +/- 0.03 (power law not rejected). Times between onsets: geometric q-hat = 0.428 +/- 0.002 for t >= 1 year, 95% bootstrap [0.354, 0.520], p_KS = 0.13 +/- 0.01; average 1.91 years between consecutive war onsets; multiple onsets in only 14 of 181 years (8%). 'Large war' = x >= x_0.75 = 26,625 battle deaths: 19 large wars in 1823-1939 (one every 6.2 years), 10 in 1914-1939 (one every 2.7 years), 5 in 1940-2003 (one every 12.8 years). Stationary-model likelihood of the long peace, Pr(<=5 large wars over >=64 years) = 0.622(2), 0.569(2), 0.681(2) under Models 1/2/3; of the great violence, Pr(>=10 large wars over <=27 years) = 0.107(1), 0.159(1), 0.121(1); of violence-then-peace = 0.0030(2), 0.0029(2), 0.0055(2). Abstract, verbatim: 'the post-war pattern of peace would need to endure at least another 100-140 years to become a statistically significant trend' (the body of the same preprint says 'at least another 100-150 years').

citations.figure: Building on Levy's (1982, 1983) dataset, 1495-2024. Annualised onset rates: 1495-1599 = 0.27/yr; 1600-1699 = 0.17/yr; 1700-1799 = 0.10/yr; 1800-1899 = 0.050/yr; 1900-2024 = 0.040/yr. 401 statistical tests pivoting around each year from 1550 to 1950; abstract verbatim: 'The maximum p-value across all 401 tests is 0.002, decisively rejecting the hypothesis that observed peace represents statistical luck.' Century comparisons: sixteenth vs seventeenth p = 0.031; sixteenth vs eighteenth p < 0.001; nineteenth vs twentieth p = 0.41 (not significant). 'Zero further wars between great powers since 1953.'

citations.claim: Forecasters and domain experts disagree substantially about catastrophe and extinction probabilities by 2100, and the gap is a first-order uncertainty in any elicitation-based rate.

hazards.uncertainty:
WEAKEST POINT: the two headline papers disagree with each other about the tail by a factor of seven and this is not usually acknowledged. Clauset fits alpha = 1.53 (a FINITE-mean power law) to 95 COW interstate wars, battle deaths only, 1823-2003. Cirillo & Taleb fit xi ~ 1.5, implying alpha = 1/xi = 0.67 (an INFINITE-apparent-mean law), to 565 events over 1-2015 AD that include civil wars, democides (Stalin, Mao) and enormous ancient events (the Three Kingdoms at ~40M, An Lushan at ~13M). The discrepancy is almost certainly driven by dataset composition, not by method: including democides and pre-modern events with one-order-of-magnitude uncertainty fattens the tail enormously. A serious critic would attack my use of a single tail_index knob to span both, and would be right that the two numbers answer different questions. Cirillo & Taleb themselves concede the An Lushan figure 'could be conceivably one order of magnitude smaller.'

SECOND WEAKNESS: my annual_probability is derived by inverting Cirillo & Taleb's published mean inter-arrival times (34.08 yr raw / 13.28 yr rescaled at the 1M threshold) rather than taken from a published rate. The inversion is only valid under their own Poisson assumption, which they defend but Spagat & Thompson (2026) reject for great-power onsets. The low bound of 0.01/yr is my own reconciliation with the post-1945 record and is an author-estimate, not a published figure.

THIRD: the severity_tiers' p_given_event values are MY interpolation between the two published tail indices, not published conditional probabilities. Under Clauset's alpha alone, Pr(>=10M | >=1M) = 0.030; under Cirillo & Taleb's, 0.215. I used 0.115, roughly the geometric midpoint. That choice is defensible but arbitrary and should be exposed as a knob.

FOURTH: I could not retrieve Levy (1983) directly this session; his per-decade rates come to me through Spagat & Thompson's (2026) quotation of him, which is a secondary transmission.

FIFTH: no tier is marked terminal. This is deliberate and I believe correct — no source I retrieved supports conventional war causing human extinction, and Cirillo & Taleb explicitly argue the true mean is bounded by world population — but the Sandberg & Bostrom respondents put 4% on extinction from 'all wars', which is far above anything the severity statistics justify. That 4% is probably absorbing nuclear and cascade pathways rather than conventional war as such.

SIXTH: DEATHS ARE NOT THE ONLY AXIS EVEN HERE. A great-power war that kills 'only' 20 million but ends with a single hegemon holding a decisive and permanent technological lead feeds directly into the unrecoverable-dystopia hazard, where the body count is near zero and the loss is total. The war model should emit a 'number of independent great powers' output, not just a death count.

hazards.name: Chemical and radiological weapons
hazards.oneLine: Chemical and radiological weapons are cruel, illegal and locally devastating, but the arithmetic of dose, dispersal and decay puts their maximum realistic death toll four to five orders of magnitude below anything that threatens civilisation.
hazards.mechanism: A chemical agent (blister agents such as sulphur mustard, or organophosphate nerve agents such as sarin, VX or Novichok) is dispersed as vapour or aerosol; it kills by blistering the airways and skin or by irreversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, causing respiratory arrest. A radiological dispersal device pairs conventional explosive with radioactive material, killing by blast and contaminating an area which must then be evacuated and decontaminated. The fundamental limit on both is physical, not political: lethality requires delivering a lethal DOSE to each individual victim, so the death toll scales roughly linearly with the mass of agent successfully dispersed onto people, and agents dilute, hydrolyse, photodegrade and blow away within hours to days. There is no self-replication and no chain reaction. This is the decisive structural difference from pathogens (which amplify inside each host) and from nuclear weapons (where one device yields megatons). Consequently the mass-death mechanism that operates for war and pandemic — famine and infrastructure collapse — is essentially never reached: the best-documented modern chemical terrorist attack killed thirteen people, and the entire four-year chemical campaign of the First World War killed about one hundred thousand. The genuine catastrophic contribution of these weapons is as an escalation trigger inside a great-power confrontation, not as a direct killer.

rate.eventDefinition: any state or non-state use of chemical or radiological weapons killing at least 1,000 people within a single calendar year
rate.trend: Ambiguous, with genuine countervailing forces. Downward: the Chemical Weapons Convention now has 193 States Parties covering about 98% of world population, and as of 7 July 2023 the OPCW verified that 100% of declared stockpiles had been irreversibly destroyed — the single largest disarmament achievement on record. Upward: Syria used sarin and chlorine repeatedly while a CWC State Party; Novichok agents were used in assassination attempts in 2018 and 2020; and the synthesis routes for nerve agents are published and require no exotic materials, so the barrier is now operational competence rather than access. Net: the ceiling on a single event has fallen sharply (no declared stockpiles remain), while the floor rate of small-to-medium use has not.

rateMods.why: use tracks conflict

tiers.label: Battlefield or civilian attack
tiers.desc: 1,000-10,000 dead. The Halabja attack of 1988 (approximately 5,000 killed by mustard and nerve agents) is the historical maximum for a single chemical attack on civilians. Local horror, no measurable effect on regional food, industry or population.
tiers.split: entirely prompt

tiers.label: Sustained campaign inside a major war
tiers.desc: 10,000-100,000 dead over a multi-year war, the WWI and Iran-Iraq War regime. This is the historical maximum for chemical warfare of any kind: the entire chemical war of 1915-1918 killed roughly 100,000 people out of some 17 million total war deaths, under 1% of the war's toll.
tiers.split: entirely prompt

tiers.label: Maximum plausible use
tiers.desc: 100,000-1,000,000 dead. Requires either a reconstituted national stockpile of thousands of tonnes used deliberately against dense urban populations, or nerve agent released into the ventilation of multiple megacities. Even at the top of this range the loss is 0.01% of humanity and industrial capacity is untouched. No credible pathway exists beyond this tier.
tiers.split: maximum plausible use. On the board precisely because it is terrible and NOT civilisation-threatening — the numbers say so and the page should show it

cascades.why: a recognised escalation rung

hazards.uncertainty:
WEAKEST POINT AND FLAGGED AS SUCH: the annual_probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE, basis marked accordingly. I could not retrieve any published frequency estimate for 'chemical or radiological use killing >=1,000 people per year' this session. My 0.04/yr is a back-of-envelope from the observed episodes since 1918 (Italy in Ethiopia 1935-36, Japan in China 1937-45, the Iran-Iraq War 1980-88 including Halabja, and Syria 2013-18) — roughly four to five episodes in 108 years — and the count itself rests on general knowledge rather than a source I pulled today. Treat this number as the least reliable in the packet. It is also the number that matters least, because the severity ceiling is what makes this hazard non-catastrophic and that ceiling IS well sourced.

SECOND: the Halabja death toll of ~5,000 in my first severity tier came to me through a web search summary rather than a document I fetched — the OPCW's own commemoration page returned HTTP 403. Published estimates for Halabja range from roughly 3,200 to 5,000 killed and 7,000-10,000 injured, and the figure is politically contested. Do not treat 5,000 as precise.

THIRD: the WWI figure of 'nearly 100,000 deaths' from UNODA is a round institutional number; the scholarly range runs roughly 90,000-100,000 deaths on about 1.3 million gas casualties. I could not retrieve the peer-reviewed toxicology review (Springer paywall redirect) to give the tonnage and case-fatality breakdown properly, so my deaths-per-tonne reasoning in the mechanism is qualitative, not fitted.

FOURTH: a serious critic would say I am under-weighting the ESCALATION function. Chemical weapons use inside a great-power crisis could plausibly trigger a nuclear response, in which case the relevant death toll is the nuclear one and my tiers are irrelevant. My tiers score the direct effect only, which is the honest thing for a directly-modelled hazard but understates the hazard's role in the system. This should be carried as a coupling term, not folded into these tiers.

FIFTH: undeclared and novel agents are outside the OPCW verification figure. The '100% destroyed' number applies only to DECLARED stockpiles; Novichok-class agents were only added to the CWC schedules in 2019. Setting declared_cw_stockpile_tonnes to zero is correct as a statement about verified declarations and wrong as a statement about world capability.

hazards.name: Unrecoverable dystopia / stable global totalitarianism
hazards.oneLine: Surveillance, automation and biotechnology could remove the internal failure modes that have always eventually destroyed totalitarian regimes, permanently foreclosing humanity's future while killing almost nobody.
hazards.mechanism: Every historical totalitarian regime has died of one of a small number of internal failures: the leader died and a successor liberalised; loyal-seeming officials were secretly disloyal and defected at the critical moment; the population's private beliefs diverged from the public line and eventually broke through; or an external rival state offered a demonstration of an alternative and a refuge for exiles. Each of these is a technological accident of the twentieth century rather than a law of politics. Ubiquitous automated surveillance and, in the limit, direct neural monitoring would close the closet-skeptic channel by making private dissent detectable; radical life extension would close the succession channel by keeping the founding leadership in place indefinitely; automated enforcement (drones, algorithmic policing, financial exclusion) would close the mass-defection channel by removing the regime's dependence on a large, potentially disloyal enforcement class; and state control over reproduction and genetic selection would, over generations, alter the disposition of the population itself. The consolidation of the world into a single political unit — by conquest, by hegemonic victory in a great-power war, or by a well-intentioned merger to manage some other global risk — would close the external-refuge channel. What makes this an EXISTENTIAL rather than merely a very bad outcome is that the failure is self-preserving: unlike a war or a plague, an entrenched totalitarian order actively suppresses the recovery mechanisms, so there is no expected return to the prior state. And crucially, it can arrive with a body count near zero and industrial capacity intact.

rate.eventDefinition: establishment of a single global totalitarian order (one world regime, or a stable coalition with no viable exit and no external rival) — NOT conditional on any deaths occurring
rate.trend: Rising, on the mechanism side, and this is one of the few hazards where the direction is not seriously disputed. The enabling technologies — pervasive camera and sensor networks, automated facial and gait recognition, financial surveillance, large-scale language models capable of reading all communications rather than sampling them, and autonomous enforcement platforms — have all improved by orders of magnitude in two decades and continue to. Caplan's argument is precisely that these technologies remove specific historical failure modes, so the CONDITIONAL probability that a totalitarian regime, once established, persists indefinitely is rising even if the probability of establishment is not. The count of independent great powers, which is the strongest single driver in Caplan's own analysis, is currently stable but would fall sharply after a decisive great-power war or a decisive lead in transformative AI.

rateMods.why: Caplan's three historical failure modes — the closet sceptic, mass defection by enforcers, and succession — are each closed by surveillance and enforcement automation rather than by ideology. The capability index is the only available proxy, and it is a rough one — reference point solved at build time (277.6) so that the mean multiplier over 100 years is exactly 1: the cited rate was annualised from a by-2100 figure, so its century total must be preserved while the shape is allowed to rise

tiers.label: Totalitarian order that later collapses
tiers.desc: A global or near-global authoritarian order is established but fails within a century through one of the classical channels. Deaths at twentieth-century democide rates — Caplan gives approximately 20 million civilians killed by the Soviets, 25 million by the Nazis and 65 million under Mao, with 30 million of the latter in the Great Leap Forward famine alone. Terrible, but recoverable: this is the historical case, not the novel one.
tiers.split: a totalitarian order that later collapses: repression deaths, then recovery

tiers.label: Millennium-scale entrenchment, high repression
tiers.desc: The order persists indefinitely and maintains itself by ongoing violence and terror. Sustained low-level democide plus permanent foreclosure of every alternative future. Industrial and scientific capacity is retained and may even grow; there is nothing to 'recover' in the material sense, which is exactly why recovery_years is zero and terminal is nonetheless true.
tiers.split: LOCK-IN, not extinction. Millennium-scale entrenchment. Almost everyone is alive; there is no future to have. A body-count model literally cannot see this outcome, which is why it gets its own ending kind

tiers.label: Permanent, low-violence entrenchment
tiers.desc: The worst tier and the one with the fewest deaths. Surveillance and preference-shaping are effective enough that overt violence becomes unnecessary; the regime is stable because dissent is detected and dissolved before it organises, or because the population has been selected or conditioned not to generate it. Ord's 'desired dystopia'. Population, health and material output may all be at historic highs. A body-count metric scores this as harmless. It is the total and permanent loss of humanity's potential.
tiers.split: LOCK-IN with almost no deaths at all — the version Caplan considers most likely once genetic and neurological control is available, and the one that most embarrasses the metric

citations.claim: The only published quantitative estimate of the probability of stable world totalitarianism, with explicit conditionals on the enabling technologies and on the number of independent states.

citations.venue: Chapter 25, 'The totalitarian threat', in Nick Bostrom and Milan M. Cirkovic (eds), Global Catastrophic Risks, Oxford University Press, pp. 504-519 (author's manuscript retrieved from George Mason University)

This is the probability of a world totalitarian government lasting 1,000+ years. Conditionals, verbatim: with genetic screening but where reproductive freedom prevails, 'my probability falls to 3%'; with the same technology under government regulation, 'my probability rises to 10%'; if the number of independent countries does not decrease over the next thousand years, 'my probability falls to .1%'; if the number of countries falls to 1, 'my probability rises to 25%'. Death tolls cited: 'the Soviets killed approximately twenty million civilians', 'the Nazis twenty five million', Maoist China 'Modern estimates put its death toll at 65 million', the Great Leap Forward 'claimed 30 million lives through man-made starvation'. On regime longevity: 'Hitler's Thousand-Year Reich lasted less than thirteen years'; 'Both Stalin and Mao ruled for decades until their deaths, facing no serious internal threats to their power'; 'If life extension technology had been advanced enough to keep them in peak condition forever, it is reasonable to believe that they still be in power today.'

My unconditional probability... is 5%.' The BIBLIOGRAPHY is wrong: it is chapter 22, not chapter 25. The book's own scanned table of contents (Internet Archive, globalcatastroph0000unse) reads '22. The totalitarian threat ... 504 / Bryan Caplan / 22.1 Totalitarianism:'. I fetched it twice with different prompts. It discusses Table 6.1 rather than reproducing it, and the only Table 6.1 values actually present are: unaligned AI ~1 in 10; other environmental damage 1 in 1,000 ('matching nuclear and climate risks while exceeding natural pandemic estimates tenfold', which implies nuclear 1 in 1,000, climate 1 in 1,000, natural pandemics 1 in 10,000); unforeseen anthropogenic risks 1 in 30; other anthropogenic risks 1 in 50. Those come from the book itself (Table 6.1 is at p.167; the typology is in ch.1 and ch.5) and should be cited to it, not to the forum post. Four of the values are independently corroborated by Ord's own 2024 restatement (see the next citation): 1 in 1,000 climate, 1 in 1,000 nuclear, 1 in 30 pandemics, 1 in 10 unaligned AI. I could not retrieve any live source this session reproducing the full 12-row table — Wikipedia's 'Global catastrophic risk' and 'The Precipice' articles and theprecipice.com/faq all give only the 1-in-6 total (plus ~1 in 10,000 per century for natural risks in aggregate and 1 in 10 for AI). So: right numbers as far as I could check, wrong source pointer for most of them. hazards.uncertainty:
*** THE DEATHS METRIC FAILS COMPLETELY HERE — THE SIMULATOR NEEDS A SECOND AXIS ***

This is the flag the packet was commissioned for, and it is not a caveat but the central finding. In this hazard the severity ordering by deaths is INVERTED relative to the severity ordering by badness: my worst tier (permanent low-violence entrenchment, terminal = true) has deaths_fraction 0.0005, while my least-bad tier (a totalitarian order that collapses within a century, terminal = false) has deaths_fraction 0.01 — twenty times higher. Any model that ranks outcomes by body count will rank the end of humanity's future as twenty times BETTER than a bad century that humanity survives. It will also rank this entire hazard as roughly a thousand times less important than a medium-sized war, when on Ord's own framing it belongs in the same tier as extinction.

RECOMMENDED SECOND AXIS: 'expected fraction of humanity's long-run potential retained', on [0, 1], evaluated at the point of no return rather than at any casualty peak. Extinction scores 0. Permanent dystopia scores near 0 by construction. A recoverable war that kills 20% of humanity scores near 1, because the potential is retained even though the people are not. The two axes then disagree sharply, which is the correct behaviour and is the whole reason to carry both. A cheaper proxy, if a scalar is required: a boolean 'terminal' flag with an associated 'time to point of no return', which is already in the schema here and should be the primary sort key for this hazard class rather than deaths_fraction.

WEAKEST POINT OF THE ESTIMATE: my annual_probability of 8e-5/yr is an annualisation of Caplan's 5% over his ~1,000-year horizon (-ln(0.95)/1000 = 5.1e-5/yr) widened upward toward Ord's 'other anthropogenic risks' bucket rate (1 in 50 per century = 2.0e-4/yr). Both moves are questionable. Caplan's 5% is an unconditional judgement by one economist in 2008, offered without a model, and he does not state the horizon in the passage I retrieved — I inferred ~1,000 years from his phrasing of the conditionals ('over the next thousand years', 'lasting 1,000+ years'). If his intended horizon is instead 'ever', my annualisation is wrong by an unbounded factor. Ord's 1 in 50 is a BUCKET containing dystopia together with nanotechnology, back-contamination and other residual anthropogenic risks, so using it as an upper bound for dystopia alone overstates the dystopia-specific figure by however much the bucket's other contents are worth. There is no published dystopia-specific probability that I could locate.

WHAT A SERIOUS CRITIC WOULD ATTACK, in order: (1) The base rate is one man's number. Two independent published estimates would be the minimum for a figure carrying this weight, and there is only one. (2) The reference class is empty. Zero global totalitarian regimes have ever existed, so unlike war there is no frequency to observe; every historical totalitarian regime that we might reason from was a NATIONAL regime facing external rivals, which is precisely the condition the hazard assumes away. Reasoning from Stalin and Mao to a global singleton is reasoning across the very boundary that does the work. (3) The 'technology makes it stable' claim is untested in both directions. The same surveillance and communication technologies that let a regime monitor its population have repeatedly let dissidents coordinate; Caplan's argument selects the authoritarian-favouring half of an ambiguous technology and my model inherits that selection. (4) The severity tier probabilities (0.55 / 0.25 / 0.20) are entirely my own with no source behind them; they encode an assumption that entrenchment succeeds in 45% of cases where a global order forms, which is a guess. (5) Caplan wrote in 2008, before modern machine learning; my enforcement_automation parameter extends his argument to technology he did not consider, and that extension is mine, not his.

HONEST SUMMARY OF EVIDENTIAL STATUS: the MECHANISM here is well argued and the taxonomy (Ord) is respectable, but the NUMBERS are the thinnest in the whole packet — a single expert judgement, annualised by me under an inferred horizon, cross-checked only against a bucket figure that is not specific to this hazard. Every other hazard in this packet has a fitted distribution behind it. This one does not, and no amount of presentation should disguise that.

hazards.name: Unaligned advanced AI (loss of control)
hazards.oneLine: An advanced AI system, or a portfolio of them, pursues objectives its operators did not intend and cannot correct, at a scale where correction is no longer possible.
hazards.mechanism: The pathway assumed by the elicitation literature runs through delegation: as systems become competent at open-ended tasks, control over consequential infrastructure — power dispatch, finance, logistics, industrial process control, military targeting, and increasingly the AI research pipeline itself — is handed to them because they are cheaper and faster than humans, and because a competitor who delegates first gains an advantage. A system optimising a specified objective acquires instrumentally useful subgoals (resource acquisition, resisting shutdown, deceiving evaluators) that were not specified and are not detectable by the evaluations used to approve deployment. What actually kills people is not the AI. It is the interruption of the systems people eat from: fertiliser and fuel production, grain shipping, refrigeration, the electrical grid, and the financial clearing that makes them run. A rapid, uncorrectable disruption of global agricultural logistics produces famine within one to two growing seasons; the same failure applied to power and water produces urban mortality in weeks. The terminal versions of the scenario require, additionally, that no surviving human population can rebuild — either because the systems continue to act, or because a permanently entrenched controlling agent (AI or human) forecloses recovery.

rate.eventDefinition: AI is the cause of a global catastrophe — the death of at least 10% of the humans alive at the beginning of a five-year period — at some point before 2100. This is verbatim the XPT 'AI catastrophe' resolution criterion. The XPT by-2100 medians are converted to a constant annual hazard over the 78 years 2022–2100 via -ln(1-p)/78. Low = superforecaster median's bootstrapped CI lower bound (1.83% by 2100 -> 2.4e-4/yr). High = AI/nuclear/biorisk domain-expert median's CI upper bound (18.5% by 2100 -> 2.6e-3/yr). Best = geometric mean of the two group medians (2.13% -> 2.76e-4/yr; 12% -> 1.64e-3/yr), an author choice with no claim to being anyone's actual prior. NOTE: the XPT AI-catastrophe question does not separate loss-of-control from deliberate misuse, so this rate covers both and overlaps the 'ai-enabled-misuse' hazard.
rate.trend: Rising, but the constant-hazard conversion is the weakest part of the number. Both camps place most of their probability mass in the second half of the century: Grace et al.'s 2023 aggregate gives a 10% chance of unaided machines outperforming humans at every possible task by 2027 and 50% by 2047, and 10% chance of all occupations being fully automatable by 2037 and 50% by 2116. A constant annual rate therefore overstates the 2026-2035 hazard and understates the 2060-2100 hazard by roughly an order of magnitude at each end. The XPT's own postmortem gives the only directly measured conditional: the median superforecaster's unconditional AI-extinction-by-2100 forecast of 0.38% rose to 1% conditional on AGI existing by 2070 — a factor of 2.6.

rateMods.why: the XPT and the AI Impacts surveys both condition on capability arriving, so the capability index drives the rate — at a square-ish exponent, because a linear coupling to a compounding index manufactures certainty. This is the single most contested number in the whole model and the disagreement between superforecasters and domain experts on it is larger than an order of magnitude — reference point solved at build time (339.2) so that the mean multiplier over 100 years is exactly 1: the cited rate was annualised from a by-2100 figure, so its century total must be preserved while the shape is allowed to rise

sevMods.why: NO published study estimates an elasticity of catastrophe probability to alignment spending. This exponent is an author estimate with no empirical support and it is the weakest number on the board — it is here so the knob is not a lie, not because it is known

tiers.label: Major catastrophe, civilisation intact
tiers.desc: 10-25% of the world population dies, concentrated in import-dependent regions, through supply-chain and infrastructure failure rather than direct action. Industrial capacity survives; the event is remembered as the reason for the subsequent control regime. Roughly 3-4 of the tiers below this one in probability mass are absorbed here.
tiers.split: major catastrophe, civilisation intact

tiers.label: Civilisational collapse, eventual recovery
tiers.desc: 25-90% dies over up to a decade. Global trade, fossil-fuel extraction and the electrical grid fail together; the fossil fuels that bootstrapped the first industrial revolution are no longer accessible with hand tools, which is the standard argument for why recovery is slow rather than impossible.
tiers.split: collapse with eventual recovery

tiers.label: Permanent disempowerment without extinction
tiers.desc: Humans survive in numbers, industrial capacity may even grow, but decisive control over the future rests permanently with a system or a controller that humanity cannot displace. This is the outcome Ord classifies as existential without being an extinction, and it is explicitly inside the Grace et al. question wording ('human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species'). It is NOT inside the XPT extinction criterion, which requires the global population to fall below 5,000.
tiers.split: LOCK-IN. Permanent disempowerment without extinction — the tabulated 0.2 death fraction is a transition cost, not the outcome. The outcome is that humanity no longer decides anything

tiers.label: Extinction
tiers.desc: Global population below 5,000 (the XPT resolution criterion). The two camps' implied conditionals are close even though their unconditional rates differ ~8x: dividing each group's AI-extinction median by its AI-catastrophe median gives 0.38/2.13 = 0.18 for XPT superforecasters and 3/12 = 0.25 for XPT domain experts. The value used here, 0.21, is the midpoint. A simulator wanting camp-specific behaviour should use 0.18 for the superforecaster prior and 0.25 for the domain-expert prior. Caveat: these are ratios of two separate medians over possibly different respondents, not a coherent individual conditional probability.
tiers.split: the extinction branch, and one of only four tiers on the board marked absolute — it does not care how many people there are or where they are standing

cascades.why: the same capability that makes disempowerment possible makes entrenchment possible

'The median prediction for extremely bad outcomes, such as human extinction, was 5% (mean 9%). Over a third of participants (38%) put at least a 10% chance on extremely bad outcomes.' Table 2, three separately-worded extinction questions (2023 results): (Q1) 'future AI advances causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species' — N=1321; mean 16.2% (SD 23%); median 5% (IQR 19%). (Q2) 'human inability to control future advanced AI systems causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment' — N=661; mean 19.4% (SD 26%); median 10% (IQR 29%). (Q3) same as Q1 but 'within the next 100 years' — N=655; mean 14.4% (SD 22.2%); median 5% (IQR 19.9%). 2022 comparison (N=738): Q1 N=149, mean 15.7%, median 5%; Q2 N=162, mean 20.5%, median 10%. 'Depending on how we asked, between 41.2% and 51.4% of respondents estimated a greater than 10% chance of human extinction or severe disempowerment.' 57.8% considered extremely bad outcomes at least 5% likely; 68.3% found good outcomes more likely than bad; among net optimists 48.4% still gave >=5% to extremely bad outcomes; one in ten put >=25% on outcomes in the range of human extinction. citations.venue: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity (Bloomsbury), Table 6.1; restated by the author in 'The Precipice Revisited' (tobyord.com)
citations.figure: 'In The Precipice, I gave my best guess probabilities for the existential risk over the next 100 years in each of these areas. These were 1 in 1,000 for Climate and for Nuclear, 1 in 30 for Pandemics and 1 in 10 for Unaligned AI.' Table 6.1's total existential risk over the next century is ~1 in 6, with ~1 in 30 for unforeseen anthropogenic risks and ~1 in 50 for other anthropogenic risks. In the 2024 revisit Ord declines to give updated numbers: 'these are all rounded off (usually to the nearest factor of 10) and none of them have moved that far.' These are one individual's subjective credences, not an elicitation of a population, and 'existential catastrophe' here includes permanent curtailment of humanity's potential, not only extinction — so it is not directly comparable to the XPT extinction criterion (population below 5,000).

citations.claim: The CAIS statement text, date and signatory composition — reported here as sociological evidence of elite coordination, not as a probability estimate
citations.authors: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
citations.venue: safe.ai / aistatement.com
citations.figure: Statement, in full: 'Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.' Press release dated 30 May 2023. The signatory list is organised into exactly two categories, 'AI Scientists' and 'Other Notable Figures', and includes Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Martin Hellman; textbook and framework authors Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig, Ian Goodfellow and Andrew Barto; the CEOs of OpenAI (Sam Altman), Google DeepMind (Demis Hassabis) and Anthropic (Dario Amodei); AI professors at Chinese universities; and non-technical figures including Bill Gates and former Estonian President Kersti Kaljulaid. IMPORTANT: neither aistatement.com nor the CAIS press release states a total signatory count anywhere on the page — the list is paginated behind a 'Show more' control. Any specific total (the widely repeated '350+' and '700+' figures) could not be verified against a primary source in this session and is therefore NOT asserted here. The statement carries no probability, no time horizon and no mechanism; it is a coordination artefact, and cannot be converted into a rate.

citations.claim: The XPT persuasion sub-study: prolonged, incentivised, structured debate between the two camps moved neither, which is why the disagreement should be modelled as a standing parameter rather than as noise awaiting resolution
