hazards.uncertainty: The 0.01 per year figure is the Hines et al. 100-year North American blackout SIZE threshold reinterpreted as a rate, which is legitimate for the size but says nothing about DURATION — and duration is what actually drives mortality. I could not find a published probability for a months-scale continental grid loss, so the tier-3 conditional probability of 0.03 is an author estimate. It is also a North American rate applied to a global hazard: European, Indian and Chinese grid statistics were not retrieved this session and the black-start composition figures are specifically NERC-registered units, so extrapolating the 60 percent gas figure worldwide is unjustified. The PNNL report itself notes a FERC-NERC finding that 'grid operators currently have sufficient blackstart resources' and that additional unregistered units exist — I have not modelled that mitigating factor and a critic would rightly say the 60 percent figure overstates the trap. Rinaldi et al. 2001 is cited bibliographically only: I could not retrieve the paper this session (the IEEE full text is paywalled and the two open PDFs I fetched did not yield extractable text), and I have deliberately attached no number to it rather than reconstruct one from memory. The National Grid restoration planning assumptions (24 hours to 60 percent of national demand, 5-7 days to full restoration, up to 14 days worst case) that circulate widely could not be verified: the National Grid Black Start Strategy PDF returned HTTP 404, so I have set restoration_days from the PNNL coal cold-start and 2003-blackout anchors instead and marked it accordingly.

hazards.name: Natural pandemic (zoonotic emergence of a novel human pathogen)
hazards.oneLine: A pathogen crosses from an animal reservoir into humans, spreads globally, and kills a large fraction of the population before immunity, behaviour change and countermeasures halt it.
hazards.mechanism: A pathogen circulating in a wild or livestock reservoir acquires the capacity for sustained human-to-human transmission at a contact interface (bushmeat handling, live-animal markets, agricultural intensification at a forest edge). Jones et al. 2008 found 60.3% of 335 emerging-infectious-disease events 1940-2004 were zoonoses, of which 71.8% originated in wildlife. Unlike most global catastrophic risks, the proximate killer here is usually the pathogen itself rather than famine: in 1918 death came from primary viral pneumonia and secondary bacterial pneumonia within days of onset. The famine and infrastructure channel only dominates in the deep tail, where simultaneous absenteeism across food, power, water-treatment and logistics workforces, plus panic-driven trade and border closure, kill more than the infection does. The event terminates not because the pathogen is defeated but because susceptibles run out: transmission is throttled by depletion of the most-exposed and most-susceptible strata long before the population-average attack rate approaches 100%, which is the single most important reason a natural pandemic is a mass-casualty risk and not an extinction risk.

rate.eventDefinition: Onset in a given year of a novel epidemic with intensity greater than or equal to that of the 1918-1920 'Spanish influenza', which Marani et al. quantify as i = 5.7 per mil per year (deaths / [global population x epidemic duration]). Historically this corresponds to roughly 20-100 million deaths over ~2-3 years. NOTE: this is probability (a) — that the EVENT occurs. It is NOT the probability of mass casualties given the event, and emphatically not the probability of extinction; see severity_tiers and uncertainty_notes.
rate.trend: Rising. Marani et al. state that 'a tripling of the rate of disease emergence, an increase consistent with the recorded recent changes, implies an approximate tripling of the probability of extreme epidemics ... bringing, possibly over decadal time scales, the mean recurrence interval of a Spanish flu-like event down to 292 y (95% CI 243 to 360 y)' — i.e. annual probability rising from 1.14e-3 to ~3.4e-3. Independently, Meadows et al. 2023 measure high-consequence zoonotic spillover EVENTS increasing at 4.98%/yr (95% CI 3.22-6.76) and reported DEATHS at 8.7%/yr (95% CI 4.06-13.62) over 1963-2019, projecting 4x the spillover events and 12x the deaths in 2050 relative to 2020. Drivers: land-use change at forest margins, wildlife trade, and livestock density (livestock are now ~60% of mammalian biomass, Bar-On et al. 2018). Countervailing: genomic surveillance, mRNA platform speed and NPIs are not in the 1600-1945 fitting window and are not captured by the stationary intensity distribution.

rateMods.why: Marani et al.'s own emergence-rate multiplier, and the cleanest lever in their paper. Land-use change, livestock density (livestock are ~60% of mammal biomass) and wildlife trade set it

tiers.label: 1918-class
tiers.desc: A pandemic of roughly the 1918 influenza's realised intensity. Marani et al. adopt 32 million deaths as 'an accredited estimate' against a 1918 world population of 1.8 billion (~1.8%); the published range spans Spreeuwenberg et al. 2018 at 17.4 million (~0.97% of world population) to Johnson & Mueller's 50-100 million (2.7-5.4% per Our World in Data). Health systems are overwhelmed regionally; global industrial capacity is essentially unaffected within a year.
tiers.split: 1918-class. ~92% prompt

tiers.label: Great-Dying-class regional annihilation
tiers.desc: A pathogen encounters one or more large immunologically naive or otherwise highly susceptible populations and kills a very large fraction of them while leaving the rest of the world near-intact. The historical exemplar is the post-1492 Americas: Koch et al. 2019 find European epidemics removed 90% (IQR 87-92%) of an indigenous population they reconstruct at 60.5 million (IQR 44.8-78.2 million) — roughly 54 million deaths, about 10% of the global population of the time, and enough to abandon 55.8 Mha of farmland and lower atmospheric CO2 by ~3.5 ppm. Note this required no prior exposure PLUS warfare and enslavement; even so, the residual 10% survived and the species was never in question.
tiers.split: Columbian-exchange-class regional annihilation

tiers.label: Civilization-stressing pandemic
tiers.desc: Attack rate and case fatality high enough, and duration long enough, that the proximate infectious mortality is compounded by failure of food distribution, power and water treatment. No historically observed event reaches this tier; it lies roughly 1-1.5 orders of magnitude beyond the Marani dataset's most intense observation and requires simultaneous high lethality and high transmissibility (see uncertainty_notes on the virulence-transmission trade-off). Industrial capacity is lost in some regions and rebuilt from surviving ones.
tiers.split: civilisation-stressing

tiers.label: Terminal
tiers.desc: Human extinction, or an unrecoverable collapse from which industrial civilisation never returns. Derived, not observed: Ord's Table 6.1 puts naturally arising pandemics at 1 in 10,000 existential catastrophe per century (~1e-6/yr); dividing by the 1.14e-3/yr event rate gives ~9e-4 conditional. This is ~333x lower than his engineered-pandemic estimate of 1 in 30 per century, and it sits about 10x below the 'likely' natural-extinction ceiling of 1 in 87,000 per year that Snyder-Beattie et al. 2019 derive from the survival of Homo sapiens for 200,000 years. A naive simulator that extrapolates the fat power-law tail without a susceptibility-heterogeneity term will land 50-500x above this figure.
tiers.split: the terminal tier, whose probability the researcher set at essentially zero — heterogeneity of susceptibility and isolated populations are why a NATURAL pandemic is very unlikely to be an extinction risk, and the model should show that rather than flatten it

cascades.why: mass antibiotic use during secondary bacterial infection
grids need staffed control rooms
weak, and kept weak

I fetched https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/Z5KZ2cui8WDjyF6gJ/some-thoughts-on-toby-ord-s-existential-risk-estimates twice with different prompts; the page is a critique of Ord's methodology. The only numbers on it are scattered comment-thread references (1 in 6,000 and 1 in 1.5 million for asteroid size bands; 3% for engineered pandemics; 3% for unforeseen anthropogenic) — NOT the table. The 'right order of magnitude ... each could easily be a factor of 3 higher or lower' quote IS on that page, verbatim, so that half of the citation stands; the numeric table does not. I then tried five further reproductions and found none: Wikipedia 'Global catastrophic risk', 'Human extinction', 'The Precipice', 'Toby Ord', and 80000hours.org/problem-profiles all decline to reproduce the per-risk breakdown. SPECIFIC HAZARD FLAG: Ord's own FAQ states that ~1 in 10,000 per century is the figure for ALL NATURAL RISKS COMBINED. The packet attaches ~1 in 10,000 to 'naturally arising pandemics' AND separately ~1 in 10,000 to 'supervolcanic eruption', which would make the natural total ~1 in 5,000. That is exactly the total-vs-component conflation an auditor should expect, and I cannot rule it out from any source I retrieved. The per-risk rows for pandemics, AI, nuclear, asteroid and supervolcano remain unverified.

hazards.uncertainty:
THE CORRECTION TRAP. Marani et al. issued a correction in March 2023 (PNAS 120(12):e2302169120): their code 'erroneously computed the number of epidemics in one year by summing the number of events in two subsequent years', inflating events/year. The famous headline numbers — '2% per year for a COVID-like pandemic', '0.3-1.9% per year for a 1918-like event', '400-year mean recurrence', '38% lifetime probability' — are the WITHDRAWN pre-correction values, and they still dominate secondary coverage and at least one search engine's summary of the correction itself, which reported the direction backwards. The post-correction values used here (0.11-0.89%, 879 y, P_Life = 0.17) are taken from the republished PDF, downloaded 18 October 2023, which is internally consistent (Fig. 2A shows 1918 at p ~ 0.55%). Two residual worries: (i) I could not retrieve the correction notice's own text — pnas.org, PubMed and Europe PMC all refused — so the direction is established by triangulation between the corrected PDF and the August 2021 press release rather than by reading the correction; (ii) the Significance statement in the corrected PDF still reads 'probability of experiencing it in one's lifetime currently about 38%' while the Discussion of the same PDF computes 0.17. I believe the Significance box was not re-typeset. Do not use 38%.

WHERE A NAIVE SIMULATOR GETS THIS WRONG. The Marani GPD has |alpha| = 0.71 < 1, i.e. no characteristic scale. Extrapolating it to extinction intensities is arithmetically trivial and badly wrong. My own calculation (author-estimate, NOT Marani's — they never extrapolate this far and explicitly restrict the MEVD to intensities above the location parameter): an event killing 50% of humanity in two years is i = 250 per mil/yr, giving (250/5.7)^-0.71 = 0.068 and ~7.8e-5/yr; 100% gives ~4.8e-5/yr, i.e. ~0.5% per century. That is ~50x Ord's 1-in-10,000-per-century and ~4x above Snyder-Beattie's 'likely' natural-extinction ceiling of 1 in 87,000 per year, though still under their near-certain 1-in-14,000 bound. Three physical reasons the extrapolation fails: (1) HETEROGENEITY OF SUSCEPTIBILITY AND EXPOSURE. Transmission burns through high-contact, high-susceptibility strata first, so the effective herd-immunity threshold falls well below the homogeneous-mixing 1 - 1/R0. Izdebski et al.'s 261-site pollen record shows this at continental scale for the deadliest pandemic on record: devastating in Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece and central Italy; negligible in Ireland, Iberia and much of central and eastern Europe. Even Koch et al.'s Great Dying — 90% (IQR 87-92%) of an entire hemisphere's naive population, compounded by warfare and enslavement — left 10% alive. (2) ISOLATED POPULATIONS. Extinction requires reaching every human group, including uncontacted peoples, remote island and Arctic communities, submarine crews and research stations. I found no published quantification of this residual in this session, so it is asserted qualitatively and should be flagged for a modeller who wants a number. (3) BEHAVIOURAL RESPONSE SCALES WITH MORTALITY and is entirely absent from a stationary intensity distribution fitted to 1600-1945.

LETHAL *AND* TRANSMISSIBLE. The virulence-transmission trade-off (Anderson & May 1982) predicts an intermediate optimum: faster within-host replication raises transmission but shortens the infectious period. Acevedo et al.'s meta-analysis (29 studies from >6000 screened) finds strong support for replication->virulence and replication->transmission, but says it 'is still uncertain if these relationships generally decelerate', and had insufficient data for the other two core relationships — i.e. the trade-off is real but only 'partial' support, and it is a soft constraint, not a ceiling. It weakens or vanishes where transmission is pre-symptomatic (SARS-CoV-2), environmental/durable (smallpox, anthrax), vector-borne (the vector, not the host, does the moving), or where the human is a dead-end host and virulence is under no selection at all in humans (rabies ~100% CFR, Nipah, H5N1). So 'disfavoured but not impossible' is the correct framing: 1918 itself combined ~R0 of 2 with a case fatality far above seasonal flu. I wanted to quote WHO's cumulative H5N1 human case and death counts as the standing example of extreme lethality without transmissibility, but every WHO and CDC URL I tried returned 404 or empty; I have therefore NOT reported an H5N1 case-fatality figure rather than recall one from memory.

OTHER GAPS. (a) The Marani dataset stops at 1945 for the intensity fit, deliberately excluding the antibiotic/vaccine era; a critic would argue the resulting distribution overstates modern risk for bacterial agents and understates it for a fast respiratory virus in an air-travel network. (b) The Black Death 'fraction of Europe' figure is genuinely contested — Benedictow's 65% / 52 million of 80 million versus Ziegler's one-in-three versus Izdebski's regionally-null findings — and my Benedictow citation is a reputable secondary reporting his 2021 book, not the book. (c) The severity-tier conditional probabilities are author-estimates constrained at the top by Ord and Snyder-Beattie and at the bottom by the 1918/Great-Dying record; the two middle tiers have no direct empirical anchor. (d) I could not retrieve the 2023 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament report — the PDF at forecastingresearch.org exceeds the fetch size limit — so no superforecaster-versus-domain-expert split on natural-pathogen catastrophe or extinction is included, and its absence should be treated as a real hole in the elicitation basis. (e) Chytridiomycosis in amphibians is the standard counterexample that a pathogen CAN drive species extinct at scale; I did not retrieve Scheele et al. 2019 this session and so state no figure for it.

hazards.name: Antimicrobial resistance (slow-burn erosion of the antibiotic era)
hazards.oneLine: Bacteria accumulate resistance faster than new antimicrobials arrive, so ordinary infections and the routine surgery that depends on prophylaxis become progressively lethal again.
hazards.mechanism: Antimicrobial use in humans and in agriculture selects for resistant lineages; horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance determinants across species and continents faster than vertical evolution alone would. The proximate killer is not exotic: it is ordinary bacterial infection reverting to its pre-1940 case fatality. GRAM found lower respiratory infections alone accounted for more than 1.5 million deaths associated with resistance in 2019, the single most burdensome syndrome, with bloodstream and intra-abdominal infections next. Six organisms — E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa — carry most of the burden. The second, larger channel is indirect and does not appear in the death counts at all: caesarean section, gut surgery, joint replacement, transplantation and cytotoxic chemotherapy are all safe only because perioperative prophylaxis works, so their risk-benefit inverts as resistance rises. Unlike a pandemic this hazard has no onset date and no peak; it is a monotone drift with a rising floor, which is why it must be modelled as a certainty with a magnitude rather than as an event with a probability.

rate.eventDefinition: A calendar year in which bacterial AMR is the DIRECT cause of at least 1 million deaths worldwide. This is already the observed state and has been since at least 1990 (GRAM: 1.06 million in 1990, 1.27 million in 2019, 1.14 million in 2021), so the event probability is 1.0 by construction. This is deliberate: AMR is a slow-burn hazard and the probability field carries no information for it. All of the modelling content sits in severity_tiers and key_parameters. Do NOT read this 1.0 as 'AMR is a certain catastrophe' — it means 'AMR is a certain ongoing burden whose magnitude is the uncertain quantity'.
rate.trend: Rising in aggregate but sharply divergent by age. GRAM 2024 finds deaths directly due to AMR among children under five FELL by ~50% between 1990 and 2021 (vaccination, water and sanitation, and paediatric infection control), while deaths among people aged 70 or older ROSE by more than 80% (population ageing, more invasive procedures, more hospital exposure). Forecast: 1.91 million direct deaths annually by 2050, a ~67.5% increase on 2021, with 8.22 million associated. The threshold question for a simulator is whether the O'Neill 10-million-per-year trajectory or the GRAM 1.91-million trajectory is right; they differ by a factor of five and were produced by scenario modelling versus systematic burden estimation respectively.

tiers.label: Current burden (observed)
tiers.desc: The 2021 GRAM estimate: 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR and 4.71 million associated, per year. Over a decade against a world population of ~8.0 billion, associated deaths are ~47 million, or ~0.59%. No loss of industrial capacity; the cost is chronic and absorbed. MRSA alone caused more than 100,000 attributable deaths in 2019.
tiers.split: the current observed burden — GRAM put AMR-attributable deaths at 1.14 million in 2021. Entirely prompt: this kills people in hospitals, not through the food system

tiers.label: GRAM 2050 trajectory
tiers.desc: The GBD-based forecast: 1.91 million direct and 8.22 million associated deaths per year by 2050; cumulatively more than 39 million direct and 169 million associated deaths between 2025 and 2050. Against a projected ~9.7 billion, a decade at that rate is ~0.85% of world population. Burden concentrates in the over-70s and in low- and middle-income countries. Still not a step change in civilisational capacity.
tiers.split: the GRAM 2050 trajectory

tiers.label: O'Neill high scenario / post-antibiotic transition
tiers.desc: The O'Neill Review's headline: '10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk' by 2050 if resistance is not slowed — about five times the GRAM forecast for the same year. The distinguishing feature is not the death count but the withdrawal of procedures: O'Neill notes that if antibiotics lose effectiveness, 'key medical procedures, such as gut surgery, caesarean sections, joint replacements, and treatments that depress the immune system, such as chemotherapy for cancer, could become too dangerous to perform'. Modern surgical and oncological medicine partially unwinds.
tiers.split: O'Neill's high scenario

tiers.label: Pan-resistant tail
tiers.desc: Simultaneous loss of last-line agents (carbapenems, then colistin — O'Neill flags 'the highly disturbing discovery of transferable colistin resistance, reported in late 2015') across the major Gram-negative pathogens, with no replacement class. Author-estimate: no published projection covers this scenario quantitatively. Mortality is dominated by hospital-acquired infection, obstetric sepsis and the withdrawal of immunosuppressive therapy. Recovery requires a new antimicrobial class or a mature phage/monoclonal alternative, not a return to the status quo.
tiers.split: a pan-resistant tail. On the board as the one hazard here that is already happening at scale and still is not remotely civilisation-threatening — which is itself worth seeing

cascades.why: secondary bacterial infection is what kills in most influenza pandemics

citations.figure: 'On the basis of our predictive statistical models, there were an estimated 4.95 million (3.62-6.57) deaths associated with bacterial AMR in 2019, including 1.27 million (95% UI 0.911-1.71) deaths attributable to bacterial AMR.' Six leading pathogens (E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa) caused 929,000 attributable and 3.57 million associated deaths. 'Lower respiratory infections accounted for more than 1.5 million deaths associated with resistance in 2019, making it the most burdensome infectious syndrome.' Regional attributable rates per 100,000: Australasia 6.5 (4.3-9.4), western sub-Saharan Africa 27.3 (20.9-35.3). citations.venue: The Lancet 404(10459):1199-1226; figures retrieved this session from the journal's EurekAlert! press release 1057804

Projected 1.91 million annual deaths directly due to AMR by 2050, with a role in a broader 8.22 million. 'Between 2025 and 2050 it is estimated AMR will lead directly to more than 39 million deaths and be associated with a broader 169 million deaths.' AMR deaths among children under five declined by 50%; those among people aged 70 or older increased by more than 80%. NOTE: the press release does not carry the 95% uncertainty intervals; the paper itself was behind a 403 and the UIs are therefore NOT reported here.

citations.claim: The O'Neill Review's 2050 projection and its economic figure — the high scenario in the tier table.
citations.authors: Jim O'Neill (chair), Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, commissioned by the UK Government and the Wellcome Trust
citations.venue: Tackling Drug-Resistant Infections Globally: Final Report and Recommendations, May 2016
citations.figure: 'We estimate that by 2050, 10 million lives a year and a cumulative 100 trillion USD of economic output are at risk due to the rise of drug-resistant infections if we do not find proactive solutions now to slow down the rise of drug resistance. Even today, 700,000 people die of resistant infections every year.' Also, from the foreword: 'today's already large 700,000 deaths every year would become an extremely disturbing 10 million every year, more people than currently die from cancer'; 'The cost in terms of lost global production between now and 2050 would be an enormous 100 trillion USD if we do not take action.' Agriculture: 'in the US, for example, of the antibiotics defined as medically important for humans by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), over 70 percent (by weight) are sold for use in animals.' Proposed market entry rewards 'of around one billion USD each'.

hazards.uncertainty:
THE FACTOR-OF-FIVE DISAGREEMENT IS THE MAIN FINDING. O'Neill (2016) projects 10 million AMR deaths per year by 2050; GRAM/GBD (2024) projects 1.91 million directly attributable and 8.22 million associated for the same year. These are not the same quantity and conflating them is the standard error in this literature. O'Neill's 10 million is a KPMG/RAND scenario extrapolation commissioned for advocacy, is not a burden estimate, and has been criticised for extrapolating resistance-rate growth without an age or syndrome structure; O'Neill himself writes in the foreword 'it is of course possible that our estimates may turn out to be too large'. GRAM's figures are systematic-analysis estimates with explicit counterfactuals. If a simulator wants one number, use GRAM's 8.22 million associated for 2050 and treat O'Neill's 10 million as the upper scenario — which is roughly what I have done in the tier table. Also note O'Neill's 'today's 700,000 deaths' figure predates GRAM entirely and is inconsistent with GRAM's own 1990 and 2019 back-estimates; it should not be used as a baseline.

ATTRIBUTABLE VERSUS ASSOCIATED. GRAM's two figures answer two different counterfactual questions — 'if the infection had been drug-susceptible' (attributable) versus 'if there had been no infection at all' (associated) — and the ratio is ~4.1. Reporting the associated figure as 'deaths from AMR' overstates by that factor; reporting the attributable figure as the total burden understates the health-system load. A simulator should carry both.

MISSING UNCERTAINTY INTERVALS. I have the 2019 GRAM figures with their full 95% UIs (4.95 million, 3.62-6.57; 1.27 million, 0.911-1.71) because PubMed Central served the paper. I do NOT have UIs for the 2021 figures or the 2050 forecasts: thelancet.com returned 403 and I fell back to the journal's own press release. Those forecast numbers should be treated as point estimates with unquantified spread, and a serious critic would attack any model that propagates them without one. The 39-million and 169-million cumulative figures in particular compound 25 years of an unstated-variance forecast.

WHAT A CRITIC WOULD ATTACK. (a) AMR is not an event, so the annual_probability field is set to 1.0 by construction; anyone summing this packet's annual probabilities across hazards will produce nonsense unless AMR is handled as a separate rate-of-loss term. (b) None of the tiers is terminal and none should be: AMR removes a therapeutic capability, it does not remove the reproductive base of the species, and pre-1940 humanity lived and grew with no antibiotics at all. Any model that produces an AMR extinction branch has a bug. (c) The pan-resistant tail tier's deaths_fraction of 0.03 is an author-estimate with no published projection behind it — I found none — and is the weakest number in this hazard. (d) The indirect burden (surgery, obstetrics, chemotherapy, transplantation withdrawn as prophylaxis fails) is the mechanism everyone cites and nobody has quantified globally; it is entirely absent from the GRAM death counts, which means the GRAM figures are a floor on total health impact, not a total. (e) Agricultural use: the '70 percent by weight' figure is US-specific and from 2016; I did not find a current global figure this session and it should not be applied worldwide without one.

hazards.name: False-vacuum decay (electroweak vacuum metastability)
hazards.oneLine: The measured Higgs and top masses place the Standard Model vacuum in a metastable state whose calculated decay lifetime is about 10^139 years, so spontaneous decay before the Sun dies is negligible and no collider can trigger it.
hazards.mechanism: The Standard Model Higgs quartic coupling lambda runs negative above an instability scale of roughly 10^10-10^11 GeV, so the electroweak vacuum we inhabit is not the global minimum of the Higgs potential but a metastable local one. Decay proceeds by quantum tunnelling: a bubble of true vacuum nucleates somewhere in spacetime and its wall then expands outward at essentially the speed of light. Inside the bubble the Higgs vacuum expectation value, and hence every particle mass and every nuclear binding energy, takes different values; atoms, nuclei and chemistry do not exist there. There is no precursor, no warning and no defence: the wall arrives at the same moment as the light announcing it. Nothing dies of famine here, which makes this the one hazard on this list whose kill mechanism is not starvation. Critically, the rate is set by fundamental parameters and is not raised by human activity — the empirical cosmic-ray bound (below) closes the accelerator route completely.

rate.eventDefinition: spontaneous nucleation of a true-vacuum bubble inside our past light-cone, given Standard Model metastability; reciprocal of the Andreassen-Frost-Schwartz (2018) computed universe lifetime of 10^139 yr
rate.trend: Flat in rate per unit four-volume. The nucleation rate depends only on the Higgs quartic coupling's running, which does not change. Human activity does not move it: the LSAG cosmic-ray argument shows Nature has already run ~10^31 LHC-equivalent programmes without producing a bubble. The one thing that could move the estimate is a shift in the measured top-quark pole mass, which is the dominant uncertainty.

tiers.label: Bubble within causal reach
tiers.desc: A true-vacuum bubble nucleates inside the region from which light can still reach Earth. The wall sweeps through at ~c. All structure inside — atoms, nuclei, the Earth, any observers — ceases to exist in the transition. No survivors, no recovery, no possibility of preparation.
tiers.split: the only genuinely and instantly unsurvivable thing on the board — a true-vacuum bubble expanding at the speed of light. Also, at a computed universe lifetime of 10^139 years, by an overwhelming margin the last thing to worry about. Both facts belong on the same page

tiers.label: Bubble beyond the cosmological event horizon
tiers.desc: In a dark-energy-dominated universe, regions beyond our cosmological event horizon are receding faster than a light-speed bubble wall can close on us. A nucleation event there never reaches Earth. This is the only branch in which a vacuum-decay event occurs and nobody dies.
tiers.split: bubble beyond the cosmological event horizon: it happens and never reaches us

citations.claim: Absolute stability of the Standard Model Higgs potential is excluded at high confidence for the measured Higgs mass; the vacuum is metastable.
citations.authors: G. Degrassi, S. Di Vita, J. Elias-Miro, J. R. Espinosa, G. F. Giudice, G. Isidori, A. Strumia
citations.venue: Journal of High Energy Physics (arXiv:1205.6497)
citations.figure: "absolute stability of the Higgs potential is excluded at 98% C.L. for Mh < 126 GeV"; theoretical uncertainty on the critical Mh for vacuum stability reduced to 1 GeV

citations.claim: The stability condition in terms of Higgs and top pole masses, and the confidence level for metastability.
citations.authors: D. Buttazzo, G. Degrassi, P. P. Giardino, G. F. Giudice, F. Sala, A. Salvio, A. Strumia
citations.venue: Journal of High Energy Physics (arXiv:1307.3536), 'Investigating the near-criticality of the Higgs boson'
citations.figure: Eq. (64): "M_h > 129.6 GeV + 2.0(M_t - 173.34 GeV) - 0.5 GeV * (alpha_3(M_Z) - 0.1184)/0.0007 +/- 0.3 GeV"; measured "M_h = 125.15 +/- 0.24 GeV"; "metastability is now preferred at 99.3% CL"; "the SM vacuum is likely to survive for times that are enormously longer than any significant astrophysical age"

citations.claim: The complete computed lifetime of the metastable Standard Model vacuum.
citations.authors: A. Andreassen, W. Frost, M. D. Schwartz
citations.venue: Physical Review D 97, 056006 (arXiv:1707.08124), 'Scale-invariant instantons and the complete lifetime of the standard model'
citations.figure: "the first complete calculation of the lifetime of our universe: 10^139 years"; "With 95% confidence, we expect our universe to last more than 10^58 years"

citations.claim: Cosmic-ray collisions empirically exclude collider-triggered vacuum-bubble production.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, 'Review of the safety of LHC collisions'
citations.figure: "These bubbles of new vacuum would already have expanded to consume large parts of the visible Universe several billion years ago. The continued existence of the Universe means that such vacuum bubbles are not produced in cosmic-ray collisions, and hence the LHC will also not produce any vacuum bubbles." Also: "Nature has already completed about 10^31 LHC experimental programmes since the beginning of the Universe" and "each second, the Universe continues to repeat about 3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments"

hazards.uncertainty: Three separate things are routinely conflated here and must be kept apart. (a) P(the vacuum is metastable at all): metastability is preferred at 99.3% CL (Buttazzo 2013), absolute stability excluded at 98% CL (Degrassi 2012) — so there is roughly a 0.7-2% chance the whole hazard has probability exactly zero. That is why the 'low' bound is 0, not a small number. (b) P(spontaneous decay per year): 10^-139, with a 95% floor on the lifetime of 10^58 yr giving the 'high' bound of 10^-58. (c) P(a human experiment triggers it): empirically zero, and the cosmic-ray argument is genuinely strong, not a reassurance — it is a measurement over 3 x 10^22 super-LHC-energy events on Earth alone. A serious critic would attack on three fronts. First, the dominant uncertainty is the top-quark pole mass, and the relation between the Monte-Carlo top mass reported by experiments and the pole mass entering these calculations carries an irreducible ~0.5 GeV ambiguity; Andreassen et al. note that 3-sigma exclusion of stability needs the pole-mass uncertainty below 250 MeV, which we do not have. Second, the entire calculation assumes no new physics between the electroweak and Planck scales; almost any beyond-SM sector changes the running of lambda and can render the vacuum stable or catastrophically unstable. Third, the cosmic-ray argument bounds bubble nucleation in collisions of a fast projectile on a stationary target; it does not by itself bound scenarios where the relevant variable is the low velocity of the produced object rather than the collision energy — LSAG addresses this explicitly for black holes but the general form of the objection (Kent 2004, 'A Critical Look at Risk Assessments for Global Catastrophes') is not fully closed. I did not retrieve a primary statement of the instability scale Lambda_I; the ~10^10-10^11 GeV figure is read off the contour lines of Buttazzo et al. Fig. 3, not quoted from text.

hazards.name: Strangelet catalysis of ordinary matter
hazards.oneLine: A hypothetical stable negatively-charged lump of strange quark matter could in principle convert ordinary nuclei into strange matter, but the survival of the Moon under 4.5 Gyr of cosmic-ray heavy-ion bombardment excludes the scenario empirically.
hazards.mechanism: Strange quark matter is a hypothetical phase of roughly equal numbers of up, down and strange quarks that some models predict is more stable than ordinary nuclear matter above about mass number 10. A small lump — a strangelet — that were both stable and negatively charged would not be electrostatically repelled by ordinary nuclei; on contact it could absorb a nucleus, convert it to strange matter, grow, and repeat. Growth would be exponential in the absorbed mass, and the released binding energy would appear as heat. The end state is the conversion of the Earth into a body of strange matter a few hundred metres across, releasing energy comparable to a stellar event. Death here is instantaneous over hours to days, not by famine. Every link in the chain is speculative: it requires strange matter to be the true ground state of baryonic matter, requires stable strangelets to be negatively rather than positively charged (models say positive), and requires them to be produced in the first place — and the empirical bounds close the last link.

rate.eventDefinition: initiation of runaway conversion of terrestrial matter to strange quark matter by a strangelet produced in a human heavy-ion collision, per year of collider operation at LHC-class energies
rate.trend: Falling with collider energy, counter-intuitively. LSAG establishes that strangelet formation becomes LESS likely as the collision system gets hotter and the net baryon density at mid-rapidity falls, so LHC Pb-Pb is less dangerous than RHIC Au-Au, which was less dangerous than the 1980s-90s AGS/SPS programmes. Future higher-energy heavy-ion machines are therefore safer on this axis, not more dangerous.

tiers.label: Strangelet produced but decays
tiers.desc: A strangelet forms and decays on the characteristic weak-interaction timescale of roughly a nanosecond, as most theoretical models predict. No macroscopic consequence whatsoever. This is overwhelmingly the most likely outcome even conditional on production.
tiers.split: produced and decays — the physical expectation

tiers.label: Stable positively-charged strangelet
tiers.desc: A stable strangelet forms but carries positive charge, as most model studies find. It is Coulomb-repelled by ordinary nuclei and cannot convert them. It stops in matter and sits inert as an exotic heavy isotope.
tiers.split: stable but positively charged, therefore repelled by nuclei and harmless

tiers.label: Runaway conversion of the Earth
tiers.desc: A stable negatively-charged strangelet stops in terrestrial matter and begins exponential conversion. The Earth is converted to strange matter over hours to days with release of nuclear binding energy. This is the branch excluded by the survival of the Moon, and it is why the headline probability is set at author-estimate 10^-15 rather than anything a survey would assign.
tiers.split: runaway conversion. Retained at a probability of effectively zero because the EMPIRICAL bound is the interesting part: the Moon has been bombarded by cosmic-ray heavy ions for 4.5 Gyr and is still there

citations.authors: John Ellis, Gian Giudice, Michelangelo Mangano, Igor Tkachev, Urs Wiedemann
citations.venue: J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. 35 (2008) 115004 (18pp), doi:10.1088/0954-3899/35/11/115004, received 26 August 2008, published 5 September 2008; preprint CERN-PH-TH/2008-136

audit.note: The QUOTED TEXT is genuine (LSAG section 5, p.11, verbatim). The ATTRIBUTION is wrong. LSAG introduces the Moon argument as 'It has been shown that the continuing survival of the Moon under cosmic-ray bombardment ensures that heavy-ion collisions do not pose any conceivable threat via strangelet production [6]' — and reference [6] in the LSAG bibliography (p.18) is 'Busza W et al 2000 Rev. Mod. Phys. 72 1125', i.e. Jaffe, Busza, Sandweiss & Wilczek, 'Review of speculative disaster scenarios at RHIC' (2000). Not Dar, De Rujula & Heinz, and not 2008. The packet has swapped this attribution with the one in the next citation. https://hep.ph.liv.ac.uk/~green/cern/LHCsafe.pdf

audit.note: Again the quoted text is genuine (LSAG p.11: 'An independent safety argument, which does not require any assumption about the velocity distribution of any hypothetical strangelets, has been given in [17]. The rate of cosmic-ray heavy-ion collisions in interstellar space is known...'). But LSAG reference [17] is 'Dar A, De Rujula A and Heinz U 1999 Phys. Lett. B 470 142'. The packet has exactly transposed the two source attributions between this citation and the previous one, and dated both to 2008 when the true years are 2000 and 1999. This is the clearest fabrication-class error in the packet.
audit.corrected: Dar, De Rujula & Heinz (1999), Phys. Lett. B 470, 142

hazards.uncertainty: The annual probability is an AUTHOR-ESTIMATE and must be labelled as such in any output. No peer-reviewed source states a per-year probability for strangelet catastrophe; the published literature states qualitative exclusions ('no basis for any conceivable threat') and empirical bounds, not rates. Secondary risk-assessment literature does quote numbers — Kent (2004, Risk Analysis) reports that Dar, De Rujula & Heinz's main bound gives p_catastrophe < 2 x 10^-8 and that the Busza-Jaffe-Sandweiss-Wilczek most conservative bound implies an expected death toll bounded by 60,000 — but I did NOT retrieve Kent or the primary DDH/BJSW papers this session, only a search-engine summary of them, so I have not used those figures as the basis. The 10^-9 'high' bound is my ceiling, chosen to be safely above any bound I saw quoted; the 10^-15 'best' reflects the Moon argument. A serious critic would attack in two places. First, the Moon argument requires an assumption about the velocity distribution of any strangelets produced in cosmic-ray collisions: those are made in a centre-of-mass frame moving at high speed relative to the lunar surface and might be broken up before they could slow enough to coalesce. LSAG addresses this and argues RHIC copper-ion data support the assumption, but it is an assumption. Second, the interstellar-accretion argument assumes strangelets do not decay on timescales much shorter than that of star formation. Both objections are honest and both are answered rather than dismissed in the primary literature, which is why I present the cosmic-ray/Moon bound as a genuinely strong safety result rather than a reassurance.

hazards.name: Self-replicating nanotechnology (grey goo) and molecular-manufacturing abuse
hazards.oneLine: Runaway self-replicating nanomachines are physically possible but unnecessary for molecular manufacturing and can be prohibited; expert elicitation puts far more extinction weight on deliberate nanotech weapons than on accidental ecophagy.
hazards.mechanism: The original concern, framed by Drexler in the 1980s, was that molecular assemblers capable of building copies of themselves from ambient matter could escape control and consume the biosphere as feedstock — exponential replication with a doubling time of minutes to hours converting biomass and crustal material into more replicators. The kill mechanism is ecophagy: not the machines attacking people but the destruction of the substrate that agriculture and every food web depend on, followed by famine, plus the waste heat of a planetary-scale exothermic conversion. Phoenix and Drexler's 2004 retraction of the emphasis is the decisive design insight: productive nanosystems need not move about, use natural resources, or undergo incremental mutation; a fixed nanofactory is an assembly line, not a swarm, and self-replication is simply not on the development path. That reroutes the mechanism entirely. The realistic chain to mass death runs through deliberately engineered nanoscale weapons in a military-competition dynamic, where the kill mechanism is conventional — targeted destruction, infrastructure collapse, and then famine — rather than accidental runaway.

rate.eventDefinition: human extinction caused by the single biggest nanotech accident, annualised from the Sandberg & Bostrom (2008) median of 0.5% before 2100 over the 92 years 2008-2100; the 'high' bound annualises their molecular-nanotech-weapons extinction median of 5%
rate.trend: Currently far below the elicited value and rising conditionally. Atomically precise molecular manufacturing does not exist in 2026, so the accident rate is presently near zero; the elicited numbers are effectively conditional on the technology arriving this century. If nanofactory-style APM arrives, the accident branch stays suppressed by Phoenix & Drexler's design argument while the WEAPONS branch — which the same survey rates ten times higher for extinction — rises with military competition. The trend is therefore towards the deliberate-abuse pole, not the accidental one.

rateMods.why: atomically precise manufacturing does not exist, so there is nothing to measure. The capability index is a weak proxy for whether it ever will, and the whole hazard is gated on a technology that has not been demonstrated. Phoenix & Drexler themselves argue the real concern is deliberate misuse of molecular manufacturing rather than accidental ecophagy — reference point solved at build time (171.9) so that the mean multiplier over 100 years is exactly 1: the cited rate was annualised from a by-2100 figure, so its century total must be preserved while the shape is allowed to rise

tiers.label: Contained incident
tiers.desc: An escaped or misused nanosystem kills at least one million people before being contained — through localised ecophagy, infrastructure destruction, or a weapons release that is not global. Industrial civilisation continues. Derived from the survey's >1 million dead threshold for the single biggest nanotech accident.
tiers.split: contained incident

tiers.label: Global ecophagy or nanotech war
tiers.desc: At least one billion dead. Either a replicator escapes containment on a continental scale and destroys the agricultural substrate over a growing region, or a nanotech-weapons exchange collapses global food and energy distribution. Death is overwhelmingly by famine and the failure of supply chains, not by the machines themselves. Conditional probability derived as 1%/5% from the survey's paired medians.
tiers.split: global ecophagy or nanotech war

tiers.label: Extinction
tiers.desc: Complete conversion of the accessible biosphere, or a weapons campaign carried to completion. No self-sufficient human population survives. Conditional probability derived as 0.5%/5% from the survey's paired medians for the same risk.
tiers.split: extinction

citations.claim: Self-replication is unnecessary for molecular manufacturing; deliberate abuse and weapons, not runaway replication, are the real concern.
citations.authors: Chris Phoenix and K. Eric Drexler
citations.venue: Nanotechnology 15(8):869, IOP Publishing, doi:10.1088/0957-4484/15/8/001
citations.figure: "Nanotechnology-based fabrication can be thoroughly non-biological and inherently safe: such systems need have no ability to move about, use natural resources, or undergo incremental mutation. Moreover, self-replication is unnecessary: the development and use of highly productive systems of nanomachinery (nanofactories) need not involve the construction of autonomous self-replicating nanomachines. Accordingly, the construction of anything resembling a dangerous self-replicating nanomachine can and should be prohibited... Since weapon systems will be both easier to build and more likely to draw investment, the potential for dangerous systems is best considered in the context of military competition and arms control."

"Number killed by molecular nanotech weapons": at least 1 million dead 25%, at least 1 billion dead 10%, human extinction 5%. Overall risk of extinction prior to 2100: 19% (median).

citations.claim: The survey's own caveats about the reliability of these medians.
citations.authors: Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom
citations.venue: Global Catastrophic Risks Survey, Technical Report 2008/1, Future of Humanity Institute, Oxford University

There are likely to be many cognitive biases that affect the result, such as unpacking bias and the availability heuristic—as well as old-fashioned optimism and pessimism."

citations.claim: Drexler's own public retraction of the grey-goo emphasis at the time of the 2004 paper.
citations.authors: Institute of Physics / Foresight Institute press coverage of Phoenix & Drexler 2004
citations.venue: EurekAlert! / ScienceDaily press release for Nanotechnology 15(8):869, 9 June 2004
citations.figure: Drexler quoted: "Runaway replicators, while theoretically possible according to the laws of physics, cannot be built with today's nanotechnology toolset" and "Self-replicating machines aren't necessary for molecular nanotechnology, and aren't part of current development plans."

hazards.uncertainty: The three quantities must not be conflated. (a) P(the event happens): not directly elicited; the survey elicits P(deaths exceed a threshold), which bundles occurrence and severity. (b) P(mass death | event): I derived the conditional tier probabilities by dividing the survey's own paired medians (1%/5% and 0.5%/5%), which is arithmetically valid only if respondents' medians are internally coherent across thresholds — medians of a population are not guaranteed to be, and this is the weakest step in the hazard. (c) P(permanent extinction): 0.5% by 2100 for the accident, 5% for weapons. The deeper problem is that a 2008 elicitation of a technology that did not then and does not now exist is measuring beliefs about a timeline, not a physical rate; eighteen years have elapsed with no molecular manufacturing, which should shift the estimate down substantially, and I have not applied that correction because doing so would be inventing a number. A serious critic would say the survey suffers unpacking bias (asking separately about 'accident' and 'weapons' inflates the total), had a small and self-selected respondent pool at a conference explicitly about catastrophic risk, and that Sandberg & Bostrom themselves disclaim it. A second critic would say the opposite: that Phoenix & Drexler's 2004 argument is a statement about what responsible developers WOULD do, not a physical impossibility proof, and that a design argument is not a safety bound in the way the cosmic-ray argument for vacuum decay genuinely is. Both criticisms are correct. The honest summary is that this is the one exotic hazard in the packet with no empirical bound at all.

hazards.name: Microscopic black hole produced at a collider
hazards.oneLine: Microscopic black holes require large extra dimensions to be producible at all, are expected to evaporate in about 10^-27 seconds, and the observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars under cosmic-ray bombardment excludes any stable accreting variety.
hazards.mechanism: In theories with large extra spatial dimensions, gravity becomes strong at TeV energies and colliding partons could form microscopic black holes. Hawking radiation is expected to evaporate them essentially instantly. The catastrophic branch requires simultaneously that Hawking radiation is suppressed (violating well-established quantum field theory in curved space), that the object is electrically neutral (otherwise it is stopped and would have accumulated in Earth and the Sun over billions of years with visible effect), and that it accretes fast enough to matter. Were all three true, a stopped black hole would slowly accrete the Earth over a timescale set by the extra-dimensional gravitational coupling; the population would die of the resulting geophysical collapse, not the hole itself. The chain is closed empirically at its far end: ultra-high-energy cosmic rays striking white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced such objects copiously, and the dense stellar material would have stopped even neutral ones, leading to rapid accretion and explosive destruction of those stars on timescales far shorter than their observed lifetimes. White dwarfs and neutron stars are observed. Therefore cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and neither will a collider.

rate.eventDefinition: initiation of runaway accretion of the Earth by a stable microscopic black hole produced in a human collider, per year of collider operation
rate.trend: Flat at zero. The bound is set by the observed population of white dwarfs and neutron stars, which does not change with collider energy or luminosity. Higher-energy machines are covered by the same argument because cosmic rays already exceed them.

tiers.label: Evaporation (the physical expectation)
tiers.desc: The black hole decays by Hawking radiation with an expected lifetime of order 10^-27 seconds, or equivalently decays back into the partons that produced it because it carries no conserved quantum number they did not. It never reaches the detector walls. No consequence.
tiers.split: evaporation in ~1e-27 s, which is what quantum field theory says happens

tiers.label: Stable but harmless
tiers.desc: A stable microscopic black hole is produced but is either neutral and unstopped (passes through the Earth), or is stopped but accretes so slowly that in seven or more spacetime dimensions the Earth survives for billions of years before any harm. LSAG treats this as the residual case and shows it is still safe.
tiers.split: stable but harmless

tiers.label: Runaway accretion of the Earth
tiers.desc: A stable, charge-neutral, rapidly accreting black hole is stopped inside the Earth and consumes it. This requires violating quantum mechanics or general relativity and is excluded by the observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars. Included for completeness only.
tiers.split: runaway accretion, at a rate of EXACTLY ZERO. Kept on the board for that reason: over 3x10^22 cosmic rays at or above LHC energies have struck Earth since it formed, and white dwarfs and neutron stars survive the same bombardment. This is what a genuinely retired risk looks like, and the page needs one for calibration

citations.claim: Microscopic black holes decay by Hawking radiation on a timescale of order 10^-27 seconds, and suppressing this requires violating basic physics.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.figure: "a microscopic black hole cannot be completely black. In standard quantum physics, the decay rate would be directly related to the production rate, and the expected lifetime would be very short, O(10^-27 s)." And: suppression "would require a violation of some of the basic principles of quantum mechanics—which is a cornerstone of the laws of Nature—in order for the black hole decay rate to be suppressed relative to its production rate, and/or of general relativity, in order to suppress Hawking radiation."

citations.claim: The observed survival of white dwarfs and neutron stars excludes cosmic-ray production of dangerous stable black holes, and hence excludes collider production.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.figure: "ultra-high-energy cosmic rays hitting dense stars such as white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced black holes copiously during their lifetimes... would have led to the destruction of white dwarfs and neutron stars on time scales that are much shorter than their observed lifetimes. The final stages of their destruction would have released explosively large amounts of energy, which would have been highly visible. The observation of white dwarfs and neutron stars that would have been destroyed in this way tells us that cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and hence neither will the LHC."

citations.claim: The scale of the natural experiment already performed, on Earth, on the Sun, and in the Universe.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 2
citations.figure: "over 3 x 10^22 cosmic rays with energies of 10^17 eV or more, equal to or greater than the LHC energy, have struck the Earth's surface since its formation. This means that Nature has already conducted the equivalent of about a hundred thousand LHC experimental programmes on Earth, and the planet still exists... Nature has therefore already conducted the LHC experimental programme about one billion times via the collisions of cosmic rays with the Sun, and the Sun still exists... Nature has already completed about 10^31 LHC experimental programmes since the beginning of the Universe. Moreover, each second, the Universe continues to repeat about 3 x 10^13 complete LHC experiments."

citations.claim: The number of extra dimensions determines whether accretion could ever be dangerous, and the intermediate cases are excluded observationally.
citations.authors: J. Ellis, G. Giudice, M. Mangano, I. Tkachev, U. Wiedemann (LHC Safety Assessment Group)
citations.venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics 35 (2008) 115004, section 4
citations.figure: "the rate at which absorption would take place would be so slow, if there are seven or more dimensions, that Earth would survive for billions of years before any harm befell it... If there are only five or six dimensions of spacetime relevant at the LHC scale, then the gravitational interactions of black holes, should they exist, would be strong enough such that their impact, should they exist, would be detectable in the Universe."

hazards.uncertainty: I report a best-estimate annual probability of exactly 0 and I stand behind it, but a simulator should distinguish why: this is not a small number rounded down, it is a chain of conjunctions each of which requires overturning established physics, terminated by a direct astrophysical observation. The three quantities: (a) P(a microscopic black hole is produced at all) is not zero — it is small and depends entirely on whether large extra dimensions exist, for which there is no evidence; (b) P(it is stable AND neutral AND accretes) requires simultaneous violation of Hawking radiation, of the Schwinger charge-neutralisation mechanism, and of the observed integrity of degenerate stars; (c) P(permanent human extinction | runaway accretion) is 1. A serious critic makes one real objection: the general form of Kent's (2004) argument that risk assessments for very-low-probability, very-high-stakes events are dominated not by the physics but by the probability that the assessment itself is wrong — i.e. the probability of an error in the LSAG reasoning may exceed the probability of the catastrophe it bounds. That objection is methodologically sound and cannot be answered from within the physics. It applies with equal force to the vacuum-decay entry. The upper bound of 10^-20 is my own placeholder for that meta-uncertainty, not a published figure, and should be marked author-estimate wherever it is displayed.

hazards.name: Extreme geomagnetic storm (Carrington-class) and grid collapse via geomagnetically induced currents
hazards.oneLine: A coronal mass ejection drives a geomagnetic storm whose induced ground currents destroy extra-high-voltage transformers faster than they can be manufactured.
hazards.mechanism: A fast coronal mass ejection with a strongly southward magnetic field reconnects with Earth's magnetosphere, driving a large ring current (measured as a deeply negative Dst) and violent ionospheric electrojets. The rapidly changing magnetic field induces a horizontal geoelectric field at the ground; long conductors — transmission lines, pipelines, cables — integrate that field into quasi-DC geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) that flow into transformer neutrals. GIC drives the transformer core into half-cycle saturation, so magnetic flux leaks out of the core and heats structural steel and windings that were never designed to carry current; Lloyd's/AER model winding hot spots exceeding the IEEE 180 degC guideline, and also model cumulative insulation loss-of-life in units that stay below it. The saturation simultaneously injects harmonics and draws enormous reactive power, which is what actually tripped Hydro-Quebec in under two minutes in March 1989. Nobody dies of the current. Death, if it comes, comes from the replacement queue: destroyed extra-high-voltage transformers are bespoke 150-400 tonne objects, and the DOE reported in July 2024 that 36-month acquisition lead times are commonly quoted with maxima reaching 60 months, so a region that loses a concentrated cluster of them loses refrigeration, water pumping, fuel distribution, sewage and medical care for months to years, and the killer is famine, thirst, cold and untreated disease.

rate.eventDefinition: A geomagnetic storm striking Earth with minimum hourly Dst at or below about -850 nT — the Siscoe et al. (2006) benchmark value for the 2 September 1859 Carrington storm, and the threshold Riley (2012) used explicitly. NOT the probability of grid collapse, which is carried by the severity tiers below.
rate.trend: The occurrence rate itself is flat to falling: Riley and Love (2017) note that 'if the current trends persist, suggesting that we are entering a period of lower activity, our forecasts may represent upper limits rather than best estimates.' Consequence severity is rising sharply, and that is where the century-scale trend lives. Transformer lead times have lengthened from the 5-12 months (domestic) / 6-16 months (international) that Lloyd's/AER used in 2013 to the 36-month typical / 60-month maximum DOE reported in 2024; the US large-power-transformer fleet averages 38-40 years against a ~40-year design life; and 82% of US large power transformer units were imported in 2019 — so a globally correlated event finds a globally correlated supply chain.

sevMods.why: the whole severity of this hazard is a manufacturing lead time. Extra-high-voltage transformers run 36 months to replace, 82% of supply is imported, and the North American fleet averages 39 years old. Hardening and held spares are the entire difference between a one-day event and a multi-year one

tiers.label: Regional trip, hours to days
tiers.desc: Voltage collapse and protective-relay cascades take down one or more control areas; a handful of transformers are damaged but restoration is by reswitching, not replacement. The March 1989 Quebec storm (Dst -589 nT) is the calibration point: the grid collapsed in under two minutes, six million people lost power for nine hours, two transformers were damaged, and the economic cost was about C$13.2 billion.
tiers.split: regional trip, hours to days — the March 1989 Quebec shape

tiers.label: Multi-region transformer loss, weeks to months
tiers.desc: Order 10-20 extra-high-voltage transformers destroyed, but concentrated: Lloyd's/AER stress that concentration matters far more than count, because a few units serving a dense population produce a prolonged outage. Outage of weeks to months across parts of one continent; excess mortality from loss of heating and cooling, water treatment, dialysis and refrigerated medicine.
tiers.split: multi-region transformer loss, weeks to months. Half prompt, half through food and water

tiers.label: Continental grid loss, 1-2 years
tiers.desc: The Lloyd's/AER extreme scenario: 20-40 million people in the United States alone at risk of extended outage, with durations of 16 days up to 1-2 years, and a modelled total economic cost of $0.6-2.6 trillion. The 2008 US National Research Council workshop report estimated '$1 trillion to $2 trillion during the first year alone ... with recovery times of 4-10 years'. At this tier, industrial food production, ammonia synthesis and fuel logistics fail across an industrialised region and famine becomes the dominant killer.
tiers.split: continental grid loss for one to two years — the transformer lead time made flesh

tiers.label: Multi-continental industrial collapse
tiers.desc: Simultaneous concentrated transformer destruction across North America, Europe and East Asia, so the surviving manufacturing base cannot cross-supply. With ~343 large power transformers per year as the maximum US domestic capacity, replacing a multi-thousand-unit loss is a decade-scale project undertaken without reliable electricity. This tier is an extrapolation, not a modelled scenario — no published study models a globally correlated grid loss.
tiers.split: multi-continental industrial collapse

cascades.why: this IS an infrastructure cascade, initiated from outside
no grid, no ammonia
cold chains and irrigation

The total economic cost for such a scenario is estimated at $0.6-2.6 trillion USD"; "If new transformers need to be ordered, the lead-time is estimated to be between 5-12 months for domestic suppliers, and 6-16 months for international suppliers"; "the mid-point estimate for the return period of a Carrington-level is 150 years, with a reasonable range of 100 - 250 years. citations.claim: Current (2024) large power transformer lead times, fleet size, weight, age, import dependence, domestic capacity, and the NERC GMD reliability standard.
citations.authors: U.S. Department of Energy (report to Congress under Bipartisan Infrastructure Law section 40103(d), signed by Secretary Granholm 10 July 2024)
citations.venue: U.S. Department of Energy, 'Large Power Transformer Resilience' Report to Congress
citations.figure: "lead times for acquisition of an LPT have become exceptionally long, with 36-month lead times being commonly quoted and maximum lead times reaching as much as 60 months"; "LPTs typically weigh between 150 and 400 tons"; "In 2022, DOE estimated that there are between 4,900 to 6,799 LPTs currently in use in the U.S."; "137 LPTs (18 percent) were produced domestically for domestic use while 617 units (82 percent) were imported for domestic use, and only 4 units were exported"; "a total maximum capacity of ~343 LPTs/year was derived for domestic manufacturers"; "the average age of LPTs in the North American grid was 38-40 years"; "The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) standard TPL-007 requires North American transmission operators to conduct studies of expected GMD impacts on their systems and take certain mitigation measures."

hazards.uncertainty: (1) The single largest uncertainty is the tail distribution, not the data. Riley and Love (2017) get 10.3% per decade from a power law and 3.0% from a lognormal on the SAME data; a modeller who picks one without saying so is hiding a factor of 3.4. My 'best' of 8e-3/yr is a judgement between them, the Lloyd's/AER 150-year mid-point (6.7e-3/yr) and Cliver's 93-year median for Dst -850 nT (1.1e-2/yr); it is not itself a published figure. The low and high are the Riley and Love power-law 95% CI bounds converted to annual rates. (2) Dst is the wrong variable for the damage. GIC is driven by dB/dt and local ground conductivity, not by ring-current strength: the 1989 Quebec collapse happened at only -589 nT, and the 2003 Halloween storms destroyed twelve transformers in South Africa at about 40 degrees corrected geomagnetic latitude, a region normally assumed immune. A simulator keyed only to Dst will systematically mis-rank exposure. (3) The NRC (2008) figures of $1-2 trillion in the first year and 4-10 year recovery are quoted here from Cliver et al. (2022), because the primary NRC text could not be retrieved this session (nap.nationalacademies.org serves page images, not text). The underlying Metatech/Kappenman scenario of ~350 destroyed EHV transformers has been contested in the literature and I did not verify it. The widely-circulated '130 million people affected' figure I could NOT source primarily and have deliberately excluded from this packet. (4) There is NO peer-reviewed global mortality estimate for a grid-collapse scenario. Every deaths_fraction in the severity tiers is my own estimate, basis author-estimate, built by combining Lloyd's population-at-risk and outage-duration figures with a judgement about excess mortality; a serious critic would attack these first and would be right to. (5) Lloyd's/AER model only North America and only transformer damage, and their $0.6-2.6 trillion is a lost-load calculation ($2.00/kW residential, $19.38/kW commercial, $8.40/kW industrial in 2001 dollars scaled by 1.31), not a general-equilibrium loss. (6) I could not retrieve the NERC TPL-007 benchmark geoelectric field value (widely cited as 8 V/km at 60 degrees geomagnetic latitude) from a primary source this session, so it is deliberately absent from the parameters rather than asserted. (7) Probability of permanent human extinction from this hazard: I assign zero and mark no tier terminal. Nothing in the retrieved literature supports an extinction pathway from a geomagnetic storm.

hazards.name: Extreme solar particle event (Miyake-class)
hazards.oneLine: A solar eruption accelerates protons to a fluence roughly ten times anything in the instrumental record, as recorded by the AD 774-775 and AD 993-994 radiocarbon spikes.
hazards.mechanism: An eruptive flare and its CME-driven shock accelerate protons to hundreds of MeV with a hard spectrum. The particles reach Earth in minutes to hours, are funnelled toward the poles, and produce a nuclear cascade in the atmosphere that makes cosmogenic radionuclides (14C, 10Be, 36Cl) — the archive that lets us see events predating instruments. The population-level radiation dose at the surface is not the killer: Earth's atmosphere is about 10 tonnes per square metre of shielding, and Thomas et al. (2013) found only moderate ozone depletion for the hard-spectrum cases consistent with AD 774, concluding explicitly that 'no mass extinction is implied'. What such an event destroys is everything outside the atmosphere and everything that depends on it: single-event upsets and hard failures across the satellite fleet (>200 MeV protons penetrate practical shielding), loss of GNSS timing and positioning, ionospheric absorption blacking out HF and polar aviation communications, and crew dose in orbit and on polar flights. Because timing, navigation and communication are load-bearing for electricity, finance and logistics, the plausible mass-casualty path is the same one as for a geomagnetic superstorm — cascading infrastructure failure ending in famine — and it is worse because the eruptions capable of a Miyake-class fluence are the same eruptions capable of an extreme geomagnetic storm.

rate.eventDefinition: A solar energetic particle event with >30 MeV omnidirectional proton fluence F30 of at least 5x10^10 cm^-2 — the class containing the five Holocene events confirmed in cosmogenic radionuclide archives (7176 BC, 5259 BC, 660 BC, AD 774, AD 993). NOT the probability of any resulting catastrophe.
rate.trend: Flat over the coming century on the available evidence. The five confirmed Holocene events show no clear clustering and the rate is estimated over an ~11,700-year archive, so a one-century trend is not resolvable. The consequence trend is steeply rising: exposure scales with satellites in orbit, with GNSS dependence of timing-critical infrastructure, and with polar aviation traffic — none of which existed in AD 774. Cliver et al. (2022) also warn the rate estimate itself may rise as the search continues: 'additional similar events may be found as the search continues.'

sevMods.why: partially shared mitigation with the geomagnetic case

tiers.label: Radiation-and-technology event, no ecological damage
tiers.desc: Hard-spectrum event as inferred for AD 774. A substantial fraction of the operational satellite fleet degraded or lost; GNSS unusable for hours to days and degraded for longer; HF and polar aviation communication blackout; measurable crew dose on polar flights and to anyone outside the magnetosphere. Moderate ozone depletion with elevated erythema and plant UV damage, but no extinction pressure. Ground infrastructure survives.
tiers.split: radiation and technology damage, no ecological effect. The five Holocene events confirmed in carbon-14 are all in this class

tiers.label: Compound event: particles plus an extreme geomagnetic storm
tiers.desc: The same eruption sequence that delivers the particle fluence also delivers a fast, strongly southward ICME, so satellite and GNSS loss coincides with transformer damage on the ground. Loss of timing and navigation removes exactly the tools grid operators would use to manage a GIC event. This is the compound scenario the risk literature is worst at pricing.
tiers.split: compound event: particles plus an extreme geomagnetic storm

tiers.label: Soft-spectrum variant with severe ozone depletion
tiers.desc: Thomas et al. (2013) explicitly ruled out a very soft spectrum for AD 774 because it would have caused severe ozone depletion and biological impacts inconsistent with the record — but ruling it out for that event does not rule it out as a future possibility. A soft-spectrum event of comparable total fluence deposits energy lower in the stratosphere and drives much larger ozone loss, with multi-year agricultural and marine-productivity damage on top of the technological damage.
tiers.split: soft-spectrum variant with severe ozone depletion — half the toll shifts to crop failure

cascades.why: the two arrive together often enough that the coupling is worth carrying

citations.claim: Atmospheric and biological consequences of an AD 774-class particle event: moderate, not extinction-level, but technologically severe.
citations.authors: B. C. Thomas, A. L. Melott, K. R. Arkenberg, B. R. Snyder II
citations.venue: Geophysical Research Letters, vol. 40, pp. 1237-1240
citations.figure: "The data may be explained by an event with fluence about one order of magnitude beyond the October 1989 SPE. Two hard spectrum cases considered here result in moderate ozone depletion, so no mass extinction is implied, though we do predict increases in erythema and damage to plants from enhanced solar UV. We are able to rule out an event with a very soft spectrum that causes severe ozone depletion and subsequent biological impacts. ... The modern technological implications of such an event may be extreme"

hazards.uncertainty: (1) The three probabilities are genuinely different here and are routinely conflated. P(event) is reasonably constrained at order 10^-3 to 10^-4 per year by the cosmogenic archive. P(mass death given event) is NOT constrained by anything published — Thomas et al. (2013) say explicitly that no mass extinction is implied by an AD 774-class event — so my severity tiers rest on a technological-cascade argument, not on a published casualty model, and every deaths_fraction is an author-estimate. P(permanent extinction) I take as zero; nothing retrieved supports otherwise. (2) The AD 774 fluence is inferred, not measured, through two chained models: a carbon-cycle model to get 14C production (a ~2x spread across published models) and a spectral assumption to convert production to fluence. Cliver et al. give both '~8 x 10^10 cm^-2' (from the 45x-1956-GLE scaling) and '~10^11 cm^-2' (summary table) for the same event; I have used 10^11 as the headline and flagged the discrepancy rather than averaging it away. (3) The rate is a LOWER limit by construction: the Holocene archive is searched incompletely. My 'high' of 2e-3/yr is my own allowance for that incompleteness, basis author-estimate, not a published bound. (4) The strongest attack a critic can make is on the solar attribution itself: Miyake et al. (2012) originally concluded that neither a solar flare nor a local supernova was a likely cause, and the solar interpretation was established only afterwards by multi-isotope work; a minority position that some spikes have non-solar or partly climatic origins still exists. (5) I did NOT retrieve the AD 993-994 discovery paper (Miyake et al. 2013, Nature Communications) directly. The 993 event enters this packet only through Cliver et al. (2022)'s list of five confirmed Holocene events, which I did retrieve. Likewise the ~660 BC event's F30 of 2.09 (+/-0.75) x 10^10 cm^-2 appeared only in search-result text I could not verify against the primary O'Hare et al. (2019) PNAS paper, so I have excluded it.

hazards.name: Nearby gamma-ray burst
hazards.oneLine: A long gamma-ray burst inside the Galaxy, beamed at Earth, strips a third of the ozone layer for years and is a leading hypothesis for the end-Ordovician extinction.
hazards.mechanism: A collapsing massive star launches a relativistic jet that radiates gamma rays into a narrow cone for about ten seconds. If the cone contains Earth, the gamma rays are absorbed in the stratosphere, dissociating N2 and O2 and producing nitric oxide, which then destroys ozone in catalytic cycles that regenerate the NO — so a ten-second input produces years of depletion. Thomas et al. (2005) model a 100 kJ/m^2 burst as giving 35% globally averaged ozone depletion, reaching 55% at some latitudes, with significant global depletion persisting for over 5 years. The killing agent is then solar, not the burst: unshielded UVB reaches the surface and the ocean's upper metres, destroying phytoplankton and damaging DNA in exposed organisms. Melott et al. note a second pathway — NO2 is a strong absorber, so the same chemistry can trigger global cooling, and the end-Ordovician extinction is associated with exactly such a rapid glaciation. For a human population the proximate killer is again famine: collapse of marine primary productivity and multi-year damage to unprotected agriculture.

rate.eventDefinition: A long gamma-ray burst beamed at Earth from close enough within the Galaxy to deliver of order 100 kJ/m^2, i.e. the 'dangerously near' class Melott et al. (2004) place at roughly 2-3 kpc. NOT the rate of Galactic GRBs, which is far higher; this is the rate of ones that both point at us and are close enough to matter.
rate.trend: Flat over the coming century — utterly flat, on a stellar-evolution timescale of hundreds of Myr. The only defensible non-flat statement is downward over cosmic time: Piran and Jimenez (2014) note the GRB rate was higher in the past and that 'life as it exists on Earth could not take place at z > 0.5', so the present epoch is comparatively safe. There is no mechanism by which anything humans do changes this rate, and no observational warning: the burst arrives with its own light.

tiers.label: Partial ozone loss, ecological stress
tiers.desc: An off-axis or more distant burst delivering well under the 100 kJ/m^2 fiducial. Ozone depletion of order 10-20% for a few years, elevated UVB, damage to phytoplankton and unprotected crops, regional harvest failures. Industrial civilisation survives; agriculture adapts with shading and cultivar change.
tiers.split: partial ozone loss. 10% prompt: a GRB does not burn you, it removes the ozone and then the UV removes the crops and the plankton

tiers.label: Ordovician-class: 35% global ozone depletion for over 5 years
tiers.desc: The Thomas et al. (2005) fiducial: 100 kJ/m^2 in ten seconds, 35% globally averaged ozone depletion and 55% at some latitudes, persisting over 5 years, plus possible NO2-driven cooling. Marine primary productivity collapses. The end-Ordovician extinction that Melott et al. attribute in part to this mechanism eliminated a large fraction of marine invertebrate genera. Multi-year global famine for a population that cannot grow food under cover.
tiers.split: Ordovician-class: ~35% global ozone depletion sustained over five years

tiers.label: Close burst, deep and prolonged depletion
tiers.desc: A burst inside about 1 kpc, or unusually energetic, driving depletion well beyond the fiducial and for longer, combined with glaciation. Loss of most open-field agriculture for a decade or more. Survival is plausible only for populations that can grow food under cover or live from stores.
tiers.split: close burst, deep and prolonged depletion

tiers.label: Terminal
tiers.desc: Included for completeness and given a deliberately small probability. No retrieved source proposes a GRB as a human-extinction mechanism; life survived the end-Ordovician event, and a species that can build enclosed food production has a survival route trilobites did not. This tier represents the residual case where depletion is deep enough and long enough that no viable population persists.
tiers.split: the tail

cascades.why: UV-driven crop and plankton loss is a food-system event by another route
