citations.claim: Independent probabilistic estimate of a lethal GRB at Earth and its dependence on Galactic position.
citations.authors: T. Piran and R. Jimenez
citations.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 113, article 231102
citations.figure: "There is a very good chance (but no certainty) that at least one lethal GRB took place during the past 5 Gyr close enough to Earth as to significantly damage life. There is a 50% chance that such a lethal GRB took place during the last 500 Myr causing one of the major mass extinction events. ... the probability of a lethal GRB is much larger in the inner Milky Way (95% within a radius of 4 kpc from the galactic center), making it inhospitable to life. Only at the outskirts of the Milky Way, at more than 10 kpc from the galactic center, this probability drops below 50%."

hazards.uncertainty: (1) The Ordovician attribution is a hypothesis and its own authors say so: Melott et al. call the GRB role 'only a credible working hypothesis'. It is not established that a GRB has ever caused a mass extinction, and there is no isotopic or geochemical signature for it comparable to the iridium layer for Chicxulub. (2) The rate is model-derived, not observed, and the two methods within Melott et al. disagree by a factor of three: a crude luminosity-density scaling gives 6 x 10^-9 yr^-1 within 3 kpc, while the blue-luminosity scaling gives a nearest-burst distance of about 2 kpc over 1 Gyr; the abstract's headline is 'two or more times per billion years'. Piran and Jimenez's 50%-in-500-Myr implies about 1.4 x 10^-9 yr^-1. My range spans these; the best of 2e-9 follows the Melott abstract. (3) Small-number statistics dominate. Melott et al.: 'Due to small number statistics, lack of knowledge of the recent GRB rate is a serious source of uncertainty in estimating the role they may have played in mass extinctions.' The papers cited date from 2004-2014; a modern Swift/Fermi-era re-derivation could move this by a factor of a few either way. (4) The severity tiers are mine. There is no published estimate of human deaths from a GRB. In particular the 0.5% terminal tier is an author-estimate placed to keep an extinction branch in the model without pretending it is measured; the honest statement is that P(human extinction | nearby GRB) is small and unquantified, so P(extinction from GRB per year) is of order 10^-11 or less. (5) Melott et al. also propose glaciation via NO2 absorption as a second, possibly dominant pathway for the Ordovician event; I have not given cooling its own tier, which understates that branch.

hazards.name: Nearby supernova
hazards.oneLine: A core-collapse supernova within about 8 parsecs strips roughly half the ozone column — though a 2024 Earth-system model argues the atmosphere shields far better than that.
hazards.mechanism: A massive star within a few parsecs explodes, delivering first a prompt gamma-ray flash and then, over subsequent centuries, a large enhancement of the local cosmic-ray flux as the remnant's shock accelerates particles that reach the solar system. Both dissociate atmospheric nitrogen, producing NO and NO2 that catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone. Gehrels et al. (2003) computed that the combined gamma-ray and cosmic-ray contribution reaches about 47% ozone depletion — enough to roughly double biologically active UV at the surface — when the supernova is within about 8 pc. The killing agent is again solar UVB on an unprotected biosphere: DNA damage, loss of phytoplankton, damage to unshielded crops. A 2024 Earth-system-model study reaches a much weaker conclusion: with full three-dimensional chemistry, compensating catalytic cycles limit the net ozone loss for a 50 pc supernova with a hundredfold cosmic-ray enhancement to around 10% globally, comparable to observed anthropogenic depletion, while the associated ion-induced aerosol and cloud forcing is comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign to current anthropogenic climate forcing. Which of these two pictures is right is the central open question for this hazard.

rate.eventDefinition: A core-collapse supernova occurring within 8 pc of the Sun — the Gehrels et al. (2003) critical distance for roughly doubling biologically active surface UV. NOT the rate of supernovae generally: within 100 pc one occurs roughly once per million years, a thousand times more often, with far smaller effect.
rate.trend: Flat. The rate is set by the local density of massive stars and by the Sun's motion through the Galaxy, both of which change on timescales of tens of Myr, so over the coming century it is constant to many decimal places. There is also, uniquely among the hazards here, an element of advance certainty: any progenitor of a supernova within 8 pc would be a conspicuous massive star, and none is known that close — consistent with Gehrels et al.'s note that no signature of such a close supernova has been found in the geological record.

tiers.label: Atmospheric shielding holds
tiers.desc: The Christoudias et al. (2024) result: net ozone depletion of around 10% globally, with polar depletion less than the present-day Antarctic ozone hole (60-70% column loss), most of the loss occurring at high latitudes, plus a cloud and aerosol radiative forcing comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign to current anthropogenic forcing. Measurable ecological stress and a modest climate perturbation; no mass casualty event.
tiers.split: atmospheric shielding holds

tiers.label: Gehrels-class: ~47% ozone depletion, doubled biologically active UV
tiers.desc: The classical two-dimensional-model result for a supernova at the 8 pc critical distance. Biologically active UV at the surface roughly doubles, sustained by the cosmic-ray enhancement over centuries rather than the years of a GRB. Sustained damage to marine primary productivity and to open-field agriculture; regional to global harvest shortfalls over decades.
tiers.split: Gehrels-class: ~47% ozone depletion, doubled biologically active UV, at 8 pc

tiers.label: Very close event, centuries of elevated cosmic rays
tiers.desc: A supernova well inside 8 pc. Ozone depletion beyond the 47% fiducial, maintained for centuries by the continuing cosmic-ray bath rather than decaying in years, so there is no adaptation window of the kind a single-shot GRB allows. Multi-century loss of open-field agriculture; survival depends on covered cultivation at scale.
tiers.split: very close event with centuries of elevated cosmic rays — the feature that distinguishes a supernova from a GRB is that it keeps going

cascades.why: same UV mechanism, over a longer period

citations.claim: A recent three-dimensional Earth-system-model revision arguing the atmosphere shields the biosphere far better than earlier two-dimensional models implied.
citations.authors: T. Christoudias, J. Kirkby, D. Stolzenburg, A. Pozzer, E. Sommer, G. P. Brasseur, M. Kulmala, J. Lelieveld
citations.venue: Communications Earth & Environment, doi:10.1038/s43247-024-01490-9
citations.figure: "Geological evidence indicates that a supernova within 100 parsecs of Earth occurs around once per million years. Such nearby supernovas can produce an intense gamma-ray burst and a 100-fold increase of cosmic rays, lasting several centuries. We find that the effect of a short burst of gamma rays is small since they are strongly attenuated before reaching the lower stratosphere. Intense cosmic radiation affects stratospheric ozone but, due to compensating effects in catalytic chemical cycles, ozone depletion is moderate and comparable to that from current anthropogenic emissions. ... We conclude that Earth's atmosphere is effective at shielding the biosphere from nearby supernovae." Ozone loss is "around 10% globally"; "The maximum ozone depletion over the poles is less than the present-day anthropogenic ozone hole over Antarctica, which amounts to an ozone column loss of 60-70%". They also record the earlier consensus being revised: "They concluded that a supernova must occur within 8 pc to have a catastrophic effect on the biosphere. A signature of such a close supernova, however, has not been found in the geological record."

hazards.uncertainty: (1) This hazard is in active revision and the literature disagrees by roughly a factor of five on the key severity number. Gehrels et al. (2003) get about 47% ozone depletion at 8 pc from a 2-D chemistry-transport model; Christoudias et al. (2024) get about 10% from a 3-D Earth-system model with ion-induced aerosol chemistry, and title their paper 'Earth's atmosphere protects the biosphere from nearby supernovae'. A modeller must choose, and should expose the choice. My tiers give the newer, weaker result the largest probability mass, but that is a judgement, not a measurement. (2) The rate of ~1.5 Gyr^-1 within 8 pc is itself derived from an OB-star census and a scale-height assumption, not from any direct count of nearby supernovae; Gehrels et al. quote competing values from about 0.3 to about 10 Gyr^-1 for 10 pc depending on the input catalogue, which is where my low and high come from. (3) There is a live third position not represented in my tiers: Christoudias et al. note that 'Fields et al. suggested that a nearby (~20 pc) supernova could intensify ionising radiation to such an extent that species extinctions can be expected'. I did not retrieve that paper and so did not build a tier on it, which may understate the hazard. (4) Only two distinct primary sources underlie this entry; the second citation object is a distinct figure from the same Gehrels paper. That is thinner sourcing than the solar entries and a reviewer should treat this hazard's numbers as the least well triangulated in the packet. (5) All deaths_fraction values are author-estimates. No published work estimates human mortality from a nearby supernova, and I mark no tier terminal: nothing retrieved supports human extinction from this cause.

hazards.name: Rogue star / stellar encounter perturbing the Oort cloud
hazards.oneLine: A passing star deflects Oort-cloud comets onto Sun-crossing orbits, multiplying the km-class impact rate for a few million years — but the shower takes ~0.18 Myr to arrive and none is inbound.
hazards.mechanism: Roughly twenty stars pass within one parsec of the Sun per million years. A star passing close enough — of order 10,000 AU, i.e. inside the Oort cloud rather than merely near it — gives an impulse to comet orbits large enough to drop a population of them to perihelia inside the planetary region. Those comets do not arrive with the star: they must fall in from 10^4 to 10^5 AU, so the shower reaches the inner solar system about 0.18 Myr after the encounter and then persists for of order a Myr as successive cohorts arrive. During the shower the flux of km-class long-period comets crossing Earth's orbit rises by up to an order of magnitude over the steady state. The catastrophe is then an ordinary impact catastrophe — ejecta, thermal pulse, stratospheric dust and sulphate loading, and multi-year global cooling that ends agriculture — with the stellar encounter acting only as a rate multiplier. Nothing about the star itself touches Earth: the Sun's orbit and the planets are essentially unperturbed at these distances.

rate.eventDefinition: A stellar passage within about 10^4 AU (0.048 pc) of the Sun — the distance Frogel and Gould (1998) take as sufficient to trigger a comet shower. This is the rate of the TRIGGER, not of an impact; impact probability is carried in the severity tiers. I computed it from the published rate of 19.7 +/- 2.2 encounters per Myr within 1 pc together with the published quadratic scaling law: 19.7 x (10^4/206265)^2 = 0.046 per Myr = 4.6 x 10^-8 per year. The arithmetic is mine; both inputs are published.
rate.trend: Flat over the coming century, and — uniquely among the hazards in this packet — verifiably flat over the coming half-million years. Because a shower takes about 0.18 Myr to arrive, any shower that will hit Earth in that window was triggered by a star that has already passed and is now catalogued. Frogel and Gould searched Hipparcos and, in agreement with Garcia-Sanchez et al., found no such recent encounter, concluding 'it is highly unlikely that one will occur during the next 0.5 Myr'. Gaia has since catalogued encounters far more completely. This hazard is, for practical purposes, currently switched off.

tiers.label: Shower arrives, no impact
tiers.desc: The overwhelmingly likely outcome. The comet flux through the inner solar system rises for of order a Myr — Cao, Loeb and MacLeod (2025) find that for a flyby at about 2,300 AU 'the terrestrial impact probability of 1 km comets increases by an order of magnitude compared to the steady state, slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale' — but no large body strikes Earth during the window in which any given civilisation exists. A spectacular sky, a research programme, and nothing else.
tiers.split: a shower arrives and nothing hits

tiers.label: Km-class cometary impact during the shower
tiers.desc: A body of roughly 1-2 km strikes Earth during the elevated-flux window. Regional devastation plus a global climate perturbation of a few years: stratospheric dust and sulphate loading, growing-season loss, and famine across the most food-insecure populations. Comets arrive faster than asteroids, so impact energy at a given diameter is several times higher than for an asteroid of the same size.
tiers.split: a km-class cometary impact during the shower — the impact-winter ladder again

tiers.label: Ten-km-class cometary impact
tiers.desc: A Chicxulub-class event delivered by the shower rather than by the background asteroid population. Global thermal pulse, months of darkness, collapse of photosynthesis, and decade-scale loss of agriculture worldwide. Recovery of an industrial civilisation, if any population survives, is a millennium-scale project.
tiers.split: a ten-km-class cometary impact

citations.claim: The shower-triggering encounter distance, the delay before a shower arrives, and the empirical result that no shower is currently inbound.
citations.authors: J. A. Frogel and A. Gould
citations.venue: arXiv e-print astro-ph/9801052 (no journal reference recorded in the arXiv metadata retrieved this session)
citations.figure: "A star passing within ~10^4 AU of the Sun would trigger a comet shower that would reach the inner solar system about 0.18 Myr later. We calculate a prior probability of ~0.4% that a star has passed this close to the Sun but that the comet shower has not yet reached the Earth. We search the HIPPARCOS catalog for such recent close-encounter candidates and, in agreement with Garcia-Sanchez et al. (1997), find none. ... we show that the search is sensitive to nearly all of the past encounters that would lead to a major shower in the future and conclude that it is highly unlikely that one will occur during the next 0.5 Myr."

citations.claim: The magnitude of the impact-rate enhancement a real close flyby produces.
citations.authors: Zhuoya Cao, Abraham Loeb, Morgan MacLeod
citations.venue: arXiv e-print 2511.11814 (PREPRINT, not peer-reviewed as of retrieval; submitted 14 November 2025)
citations.figure: "For the closest approach (b ~ 2,300 AU), the terrestrial impact probability of 1 km comets increases by an order of magnitude compared to the steady state, slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale. ... We identify a threshold diameter D_0 = 2.25 km for which yields P = 1 in our model, with D_0 following a logarithmic dependence on b." Context: HD7977's encounter 2.47 Myr ago, 'with possible flyby distances ranging from 2,300 AU to ~13,000 AU'.

hazards.uncertainty: (1) The headline annual probability is MY arithmetic, not a published figure, and is flagged basis 'author-estimate' for that reason. I combined two published inputs — the 19.7 +/- 2.2 per Myr rate within 1 pc and the published quadratic scaling — with Frogel and Gould's 10^4 AU threshold. If the true shower threshold is 5,000 AU rather than 10^4 AU the rate falls by a factor of four; if it is 20,000 AU it rises by four. Nothing I retrieved pins that threshold tightly. (2) The severity tiers are the weakest part of this entry. I had no retrieved source for the BACKGROUND km-class impact rate, so the impact probabilities within the shower window (2.8% and 0.2%) are author-estimates constructed from the order-of-magnitude enhancement figure and a rough shower duration. Do not treat 0.028 and 0.002 as literature values; replace them with a proper convolution against a sourced impact-frequency curve. (3) The enhancement magnitude rests on 2025 arXiv preprints that have not been peer reviewed. The Bailer-Jones encounter rate is solid; the impact multiplier is not. (4) This hazard has a property none of the others share and which a simulator must not lose: it is currently OFF and known to be off. Frogel and Gould's null search, now vastly strengthened by Gaia, means no shower can reach Earth for roughly the next 0.5 Myr. Sampling this as a memoryless Poisson process every year is wrong in a way that matters — the correct implementation gates on the observed stellar census. (5) A serious critic would also attack the premise that comet showers matter at all relative to the asteroid background: Cao et al. find the enhanced 1-km comet probability only 'slightly exceeding the asteroid impact probability at this size scale', i.e. even a strong shower roughly doubles the total km-class hazard rather than dominating it.
